language.name: JavaScript
language.description: The language of the web and the base of the MERN stack. Covers types and coercion, scope and closures, functions and this, objects, classes, arrays, modern ES features, async code and the event loop, the DOM, performance, and the coding challenges interviewers love.

questions.question: What are the data types in JavaScript?
questions.answer:
Short answer: JavaScript has 7 primitive types (string, number, bigint, boolean, undefined, null, symbol) and one non-primitive type, object. Arrays, functions, dates and maps are all objects.

How it works:
string: text, like "Ali"
number: integers and decimals share one type, like 42 and 3.14
bigint: whole numbers bigger than 2^53, like 9007199254740993n
boolean: true or false
undefined: a variable that has no value yet
null: an empty value you set on purpose
symbol: a unique id, often used as a hidden object key
object: everything else, including arrays and functions

Example: In a user profile, name is a string, age is a number, isAdmin is a boolean, address is an object and skills is an array (also an object).

Common mistake: Saying "array" and "function" are separate types. typeof [] is "object", and functions are special objects (typeof gives "function").

Interview tip: Group them as "7 primitives plus objects", then say primitives are copied by value and objects by reference. That leads naturally into the next question interviewers usually ask.
questions.codeSnippet:
typeof 'Ali';      // "string"
typeof 42;         // "number"
typeof 10n;        // "bigint"
typeof undefined;  // "undefined"
typeof null;       // "object"  (old bug)
typeof [];         // "object"
typeof (() => {}); // "function"

questions.question: What is the difference between var, let and const?
questions.answer:
Short answer: var is function-scoped and can be redeclared. let and const are block-scoped. const cannot be reassigned, while let can. Modern code uses const by default and let when the value must change.

How it works:
var: function scope, hoisted as undefined, can be redeclared
let: block scope ({ }), hoisted but not usable before its line (temporal dead zone)
const: like let, but must be assigned once and never reassigned
Global var: becomes a property of window in browser scripts

Example: In a for loop with var i, the same i is shared after the loop ends. With let i, each loop run gets its own i, which is why closures inside loops work correctly with let.

Common mistake: Thinking const makes a value unchangeable. const user = { name: 'Ali' } still allows user.name = 'Sara'. Only the variable cannot point to a new object.

Interview tip: Say your rule: "const by default, let when I need to reassign, never var in new code". Then explain the loop example, which shows you understand scope, not just syntax.

questions.question: What is the difference between primitive and reference values when you copy or compare them?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Primitives are copied by value, so a copy is fully separate. Objects are copied by reference, so two variables can point to the same object, and changing it through one changes it for both.

How it works:
Copy a primitive: let b = a creates a new independent value
Copy an object: let b = a copies the address, not the object
Compare primitives: by value, 5 === 5 is true
Compare objects: by reference, {} === {} is false
Functions: receive a copy of the reference, so they can change the caller's object

Example: A React state update does user.name = 'Sara' then setUser(user). React sees the same reference, thinks nothing changed and does not re-render. setUser({ ...user, name: 'Sara' }) creates a new object and works.

Common mistake: Copying an array with const copy = arr and then sorting copy. The original array is sorted too, because there is only one array.

Interview tip: Use the "house address" analogy: copying an object variable copies the address on a paper, not the house. Then link it to React state immutability, which interviewers love.

questions.question: What is the difference between null and undefined?
questions.answer:
Short answer: undefined means a value was never set. null means "no value" set on purpose by the programmer. Both are falsy and both mean "nothing", but they come from different places.

How it works:
undefined: a declared variable with no value, a missing object property, a missing function argument, a function with no return
null: you assign it to clear something, like user = null after logout
typeof: undefined gives "undefined", null gives "object" (a historic bug)
Equality: null == undefined is true, null === undefined is false
JSON: undefined properties are dropped, null is kept

Example: An API returns { middleName: null } to say "this user has no middle name", while a missing middleName field means the API did not send it at all.

Common mistake: Checking only one of them, like if (value === null), and missing undefined. value == null catches both in one check, and it is one of the few good uses of ==.

Interview tip: Mention that default parameters and ?? treat them differently: default parameters only apply for undefined, while ?? applies for both null and undefined.

questions.question: What does typeof return for each type, and what are its famous quirks?
questions.answer:
Short answer: typeof returns a string naming the type of a value. It works well for primitives and functions, but it says "object" for null and for arrays, so you need other checks for those.

How it works: The quirks:
typeof null: "object", a bug kept since 1995 for compatibility
typeof []: "object", use Array.isArray() instead
typeof NaN: "number", NaN is a special number value
typeof function: "function", even though functions are objects
typeof undeclaredVariable: "undefined", no error, unlike reading it

Example: A helper does if (typeof data === 'object') data.items.map(...). When the API returns null, the check passes and the code crashes with "Cannot read properties of null".

Common mistake: Writing typeof x === 'array'. That is never true, so the branch never runs.

Interview tip: Show the safe checks together: x === null, Array.isArray(x), Number.isNaN(x), and typeof for the rest. Knowing the right tool for each case is what interviewers check.
questions.codeSnippet:
const isPlainObject = (v) => v !== null && typeof v === 'object' && !Array.isArray(v);

isPlainObject({});    // true
isPlainObject(null);  // false
isPlainObject([]);    // false

questions.question: If const does not make an object immutable, how do you make an object truly read-only?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Use Object.freeze(). It stops adding, removing and changing properties. But it is shallow: nested objects inside are still changeable unless you freeze them too.

How it works:
const: the variable cannot point to something else
Object.freeze(obj): properties cannot be added, deleted or changed
Shallow: obj.inner.x = 1 still works on a nested object
Strict mode: changing a frozen object throws a TypeError, in sloppy mode it fails silently
Deep freeze: a small recursive function, or libraries like Immer

Example: A config object const ROLES = Object.freeze({ ADMIN: 'admin', USER: 'user' }) stops anyone from doing ROLES.ADMIN = 'x' by mistake somewhere in the code.

Common mistake: Freezing state objects and expecting nested arrays to be protected. settings.themes.push('dark') still works on a frozen settings object.

Interview tip: Mention Object.seal() too: it blocks adding and deleting properties but still allows changing existing values. Comparing const, seal and freeze in one sentence shows depth.

questions.question: Why is 0.1 + 0.2 not equal to 0.3 in JavaScript, and how do you handle money safely?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Numbers are stored as 64-bit binary floating point (IEEE 754). Most decimal fractions like 0.1 cannot be stored exactly in binary, so tiny errors appear. For money, store whole paisa or cents as integers, or use a decimal library.

How it works:
Binary storage: 0.1 is stored as 0.1000000000000000055...
Result: 0.1 + 0.2 gives 0.30000000000000004
Safe integers: whole numbers up to 2^53 - 1 are exact
Comparing decimals: use Math.abs(a - b) < Number.EPSILON for small values
Showing money: toFixed(2) or Intl.NumberFormat, only for display

Example: A cart adds 3 items at Rs 0.10 each in floating point and shows Rs 0.30000000000000004. Storing 10 paisa as the integer 10, adding to 30, and dividing by 100 only for display gives exactly Rs 0.30.

Common mistake: Rounding with toFixed in the middle of calculations. toFixed returns a string, and repeated rounding adds its own errors.

Interview tip: Say this is not a JavaScript bug, Python and Java doubles do the same. Then give the integer-cents solution. Calm, practical answers like that impress.
questions.codeSnippet:
console.log(0.1 + 0.2);            // 0.30000000000000004
console.log(0.1 + 0.2 === 0.3);    // false

const totalPaisa = 10 + 20;        // store money as integers
console.log((totalPaisa / 100).toFixed(2)); // "0.30"

questions.question: What are BigInt and Symbol used for in real JavaScript code?
questions.answer:
Short answer: BigInt stores whole numbers larger than Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER without losing precision. Symbol creates a unique value, mostly used as object keys that never clash and as hooks into built-in behaviour.

How it works:
BigInt: write 123n or BigInt('123'), cannot mix with normal numbers in math
BigInt use: database ids from other systems, money in the smallest unit, cryptography
Symbol(): every call gives a new unique value, even with the same description
Well-known symbols: Symbol.iterator makes an object usable in for...of
Symbol keys: skipped by JSON.stringify and for...in

Example: A Twitter-style id 1234567890123456789 read as a normal number becomes 1234567890123456800, pointing to the wrong record. Keeping it as a string or a BigInt keeps it correct.

Common mistake: Writing 10n + 5. Mixing BigInt and Number throws a TypeError, so convert one side first.

Interview tip: Mention that JSON.stringify cannot handle BigInt by default (it throws), so APIs usually send big ids as strings. This detail shows real-world experience.

questions.question: How do you reliably check the type of a value in JavaScript?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Use the right check for each kind: typeof for most primitives and functions, === null for null, Array.isArray for arrays, Number.isNaN for NaN, and instanceof or Object.prototype.toString for other objects.

How it works:
Primitives: typeof x === 'string', 'number', 'boolean', 'bigint', 'symbol'
null: x === null
Array: Array.isArray(x), works even across iframes
NaN: Number.isNaN(x), not the global isNaN
Date and others: x instanceof Date, or Object.prototype.toString.call(x) gives "[object Date]"
Finite number: Number.isFinite(x) rejects NaN and Infinity

Example: Validating a request body in Node: typeof body.age === 'number' && Number.isFinite(body.age) && body.age >= 0 rejects "25", NaN, Infinity and -1 in one line.

Common mistake: Using the global isNaN('abc'). It converts the string first and returns true, while Number.isNaN('abc') is false because "abc" is not the NaN value.

Interview tip: Mention that for larger apps you use a schema library like zod instead of hand-written checks, but you still know what it does underneath.
questions.codeSnippet:
Object.prototype.toString.call([]);         // "[object Array]"
Object.prototype.toString.call(new Date()); // "[object Date]"
Object.prototype.toString.call(null);       // "[object Null]"
isNaN('abc');          // true  (converts first)
Number.isNaN('abc');   // false

questions.question: What does "use strict" change in JavaScript, and when is strict mode on automatically?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Strict mode turns silent mistakes into errors and removes some confusing features. It is on automatically inside ES modules and class bodies, so most modern code already runs in strict mode.

How it works: Main changes:
Undeclared variables: x = 5 throws instead of creating a global
this in plain function calls: undefined instead of the global object
Read-only properties: writing to a frozen object throws
Duplicate parameter names: a SyntaxError
with statement: not allowed
Automatic: files using import/export, type="module" scripts, and class bodies

Example: A typo like usre = data inside a function silently creates a global variable in sloppy mode. In strict mode it throws "usre is not defined", and you find the bug in seconds.

Common mistake: Adding "use strict" in the middle of a file. It only works as the first statement of a script or function.

Interview tip: Mention that Node CommonJS files are not strict by default, while ES modules are. This shows you know where your code actually runs.

questions.question: Which of these is NOT a primitive type in JavaScript?
questions.answer:
Why C: object is the one non-primitive type. Arrays and functions are objects too.

Why not A: string is a primitive.

Why not B: symbol is a primitive added in ES6.

Why not D: bigint is a primitive added in ES2020.

questions.question: What does typeof null return?
questions.answer:
Why C: It is a famous bug from the first version of JavaScript, kept so old websites do not break.

Why not A: There is no "null" result from typeof.

Why not B: "undefined" is returned for undefined values, not null.

Why not D: typeof never throws for null.

questions.question: What happens with const arr = [1, 2]; arr.push(3);?
questions.answer:
Why B: const blocks reassigning the variable, not changing the array it points to. push changes the same array.

Why not A: That error comes from arr = something, a reassignment.

Why not C: The push really happens.

Why not D: The code is valid syntax.

questions.question: After let a = { x: 1 }; let b = a; b.x = 2;, what is a.x?
questions.answer:
Why D: a and b hold the same reference, so changing the object through b changes it for a too.

Why not A: That would be true only if b were a copy, like { ...a }.

Why not B: The property exists and has a value.

Why not C: Changing a property of an object is allowed.

questions.question: What does typeof NaN return?
questions.answer:
Why B: NaN ("Not a Number") is a special value of the number type, used for failed math like 0 / 0.

Why not A: typeof never returns "NaN".

Why not C: NaN is a real value, not undefined.

Why not D: Only null and objects give "object".

questions.question: What does 9007199254740992 === 9007199254740993 return?
questions.answer:
Why C: Both are above Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER (9007199254740991), so 9007199254740993 cannot be stored exactly and becomes 9007199254740992.

Why not A: That would be true with BigInt literals (with an n at the end).

Why not B: JavaScript never throws for large numbers, it loses precision silently.

Why not D: A comparison always returns true or false.

questions.question: What is the difference between == and === in JavaScript?
questions.answer:
Short answer: === (strict equality) compares value and type, with no conversion. == (loose equality) first converts the values to a common type, then compares. That conversion causes surprising results, so most code uses ===.

How it works:
5 === '5': false, different types
5 == '5': true, the string becomes a number first
0 == false: true, false becomes 0
null == undefined: true, a special rule
null == 0: false, null only loosely equals undefined

Example: A form gives age as the string "18". if (age === 18) is false and the user is blocked. Convert first with Number(age), then compare with ===.

Common mistake: Thinking == is "wrong" everywhere. value == null is a common, clear way to check for both null and undefined at once, and many style guides allow exactly that one case.

Interview tip: Say "I use === by default and convert types myself, so the code says what it means". Then mention the == null exception. Interviewers like both the rule and the nuance.
questions.codeSnippet:
console.log(5 === '5');          // false
console.log(5 == '5');           // true
console.log(0 == false);         // true
console.log(null == undefined);  // true
console.log(null == 0);          // false

questions.question: Which values are falsy in JavaScript, and why does it matter?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Only a few values are falsy: false, 0, -0, 0n, "" (empty string), null, undefined and NaN. Everything else is truthy, including "0", "false", [] and {}.

How it works:
Falsy: these values become false in if, &&, || and !
Truthy: every object, every non-empty string, every non-zero number
Surprises: "0" and " " are truthy strings, [] and {} are truthy objects
Double bang: !!value converts any value to a real boolean

Example: if (cart.items) shows the cart even when items is [], because an empty array is truthy. The correct check is if (cart.items.length > 0).

Common mistake: Writing count || 10 for a default. When count is a valid 0, it is falsy and gets replaced by 10. Use count ?? 10, which only replaces null and undefined.

Interview tip: List the falsy values from memory and add "everything else is truthy". Then show the || vs ?? example. It is short and shows real coding experience.

questions.question: How does the + operator decide between adding numbers and joining strings?
questions.answer:
Short answer: If either side is a string (after converting objects to primitives), + joins them as strings. Otherwise it adds them as numbers. The other math operators (-, *, /) always convert to numbers.

How it works:
1 + 2: 3
'1' + 2: "12", a string on one side wins
1 + 2 + '3': "33", left to right, 1 + 2 first
'3' - 1: 2, minus always converts to numbers
+'42': 42, unary plus converts to a number
true + 1: 2, true becomes 1

Example: Two input fields have the values "5" and "10". a + b shows "510" instead of 15, because input values are always strings. Number(a) + Number(b) gives 15.

Common mistake: Building a total in a loop with total += item.price where some prices came from an API as strings. One string turns the whole total into a long joined string.

Interview tip: Mention that you convert input at the boundary (form, API, query string) once, so the rest of the code works only with real numbers.
questions.codeSnippet:
console.log(1 + 2);        // 3
console.log('1' + 2);      // "12"
console.log(1 + 2 + '3');  // "33"
console.log('3' - 1);      // 2
console.log(+'42');        // 42

questions.question: What is NaN, why is NaN !== NaN, and how should you check for it?
questions.answer:
Short answer: NaN means "Not a Number", the result of failed numeric operations like Number("abc") or 0 / 0. By the floating point rules, NaN is not equal to anything, even itself. Check it with Number.isNaN().

How it works:
Creating NaN: Number('abc'), parseInt('px'), Math.sqrt(-1), 0 / 0
Comparison: NaN === NaN is false, NaN == NaN is false
Number.isNaN(x): true only for the real NaN value
isNaN(x): converts first, so isNaN('hello') is true
Object.is(NaN, NaN): true
Array: [NaN].includes(NaN) is true, [NaN].indexOf(NaN) is -1

Example: A price parser returns NaN for "Rs 500". Later, NaN > 0 and NaN < 0 are both false, so the item slips past every validation check and shows "NaN" on the invoice.

Common mistake: Writing if (value === NaN). It is never true, so the check never catches anything.

Interview tip: Mention that NaN spreads: any math with NaN gives NaN. That is why you validate numbers right after parsing, not at the end of a long calculation.
questions.codeSnippet:
const price = Number('Rs 500');
console.log(price);               // NaN
console.log(price === NaN);       // false
console.log(Number.isNaN(price)); // true
console.log([NaN].includes(NaN)); // true
console.log([NaN].indexOf(NaN));  // -1

questions.question: What is the difference between Number(), parseInt(), parseFloat() and the unary + for converting strings?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Number() and unary + convert the whole string and give NaN if any part is not numeric. parseInt() and parseFloat() read from the start and stop at the first invalid character, so "12px" becomes 12.

How it works:
Number('12px'): NaN, whole string must be valid
parseInt('12px'): 12, stops at "p"
parseFloat('3.5kg'): 3.5
Number(''): 0, a famous trap
parseInt(''): NaN
parseInt('08'): 8, always pass the radix to be clear, parseInt(x, 10)

Example: Reading a CSS value, parseInt(getComputedStyle(el).width, 10) turns "250px" into 250. For a quantity field, Number(input) is better, because "5abc" should be rejected, not quietly read as 5.

Common mistake: Using ['1', '2', '3'].map(parseInt). map passes the index as the second argument (the radix), so the result is [1, NaN, NaN].

Interview tip: Say you use Number() for strict validation and parseInt with radix 10 only when you expect units or trailing text.
questions.codeSnippet:
console.log(Number('12px'));            // NaN
console.log(parseInt('12px', 10));      // 12
console.log(Number(''));                // 0
console.log(['1', '2', '3'].map(parseInt)); // [1, NaN, NaN]
console.log(['1', '2', '3'].map(Number));   // [1, 2, 3]

questions.question: What is the difference between Object.is() and ===?
questions.answer:
Short answer: They are the same except for two cases: Object.is(NaN, NaN) is true (=== says false), and Object.is(0, -0) is false (=== says true). Object.is is "same value" equality.

How it works:
NaN: === false, Object.is true
+0 and -0: === true, Object.is false
Everything else: identical results
Who uses it: React compares state and dependencies with Object.is

Example: In React, setCount(NaN) twice in a row does not cause a second re-render, because Object.is(NaN, NaN) is true. With === React would re-render every time.

Common mistake: Thinking Object.is compares objects deeply. Object.is({}, {}) is still false, because they are different objects.

Interview tip: Mention the React connection. Linking a small language detail to a framework you use every day shows you understand why the detail matters.
questions.codeSnippet:
console.log(NaN === NaN);           // false
console.log(Object.is(NaN, NaN));   // true
console.log(0 === -0);              // true
console.log(Object.is(0, -0));      // false
console.log(Object.is({}, {}));     // false

questions.question: How does JavaScript convert an object to a primitive, and why does [] + {} give "[object Object]"?
questions.answer:
Short answer: When an object is used with + or compared, JavaScript calls Symbol.toPrimitive if it exists, otherwise valueOf() and then toString(). For [] that gives "" and for {} it gives "[object Object]", so "" + "[object Object]" is "[object Object]".

How it works:
Hint: "number" for math, "string" for template literals, "default" for + and ==
valueOf(): for plain objects and arrays it returns the object itself, so it is skipped
toString(): [] gives "", [1, 2] gives "1,2", {} gives "[object Object]"
Dates: use toString for + and valueOf (milliseconds) for -
Your own objects: define Symbol.toPrimitive to control it

Example: A Money class with Symbol.toPrimitive returns the amount for math and "Rs 500" for strings, so `${price}` prints nicely and price * 2 still works.

Common mistake: Logging "User: " + user and getting "User: [object Object]". Use JSON.stringify(user) or a template literal with specific fields.

Interview tip: Walk through the steps out loud for one example. Interviewers ask these puzzles to see your reasoning, not whether you memorized the answer.

questions.question: Why is [] == ![] true in JavaScript? Explain it step by step.
questions.answer:
Short answer: ![] is false, because [] is truthy. Then [] == false converts both sides to numbers: false becomes 0, and [] becomes "" and then 0. So 0 == 0 is true.

How it works: Step by step:
Step 1: ![] is evaluated first, [] is truthy, so it becomes false
Step 2: [] == false, a boolean on one side converts to a number, 0
Step 3: [] == 0, an object compared with a number becomes a primitive
Step 4: [].toString() is "", so "" == 0
Step 5: "" converts to the number 0, and 0 == 0 is true

Example: This is a famous interview puzzle, but the same rules cause real bugs, like if (items == false) being true for an empty array, a "0" string and the number 0.

Common mistake: Guessing from intuition ("an array cannot equal its opposite"). Coercion rules are mechanical, so the only reliable way is to follow the steps.

Interview tip: Finish with "this is exactly why I use === in real code". Solving the puzzle and then giving the practical lesson is the ideal answer.
questions.codeSnippet:
console.log(![]);        // false
console.log([] == false); // true
console.log([] == 0);     // true
console.log([] == ![]);   // true

questions.question: A form sends age as "25". The code does if (age > 18) and later age + 1, and the result shows "251". What is happening?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Values from inputs, query strings and localStorage are strings. > converts the string to a number, so the check works, but + joins strings, so "25" + 1 becomes "251". The same variable behaves like a number in one place and a string in another.

How it works:
age > 18: comparison with a number converts "25" to 25, true
age + 1: one side is a string, so it joins, "251"
age - 1: minus converts, 24
Fix: convert once at the boundary, const age = Number(form.age)
Validate: Number.isInteger(age) && age > 0

Example: A real signup page shows "You will be 251 next year!" because of this. Unit tests passed, since they used the number 25 instead of the string the browser really sends.

Common mistake: Fixing it only where the bug was noticed, like age * 1 + 1. Other parts of the code still get the string and break later.

Interview tip: Mention that every value from outside (forms, URL, localStorage, JSON from untrusted sources) is untrusted input that you parse and validate once. It shows clean architecture thinking.

questions.question: How do comparison operators like < and > behave with strings, numbers and mixed types?
questions.answer:
Short answer: If both sides are strings, they are compared character by character by their character codes (dictionary order). If either side is not a string, both are converted to numbers first. This is why "10" < "9" is true but "10" < 9 is false.

How it works:
"10" < "9": both strings, "1" comes before "9", true
"10" < 9: one number, "10" becomes 10, false
"apple" < "banana": dictionary order, true
"Zebra" < "apple": capital letters come first in code order, true
null >= 0: null becomes 0, true (but null == 0 is false)
undefined < 1: undefined becomes NaN, false

Example: Sorting version strings like "1.10" and "1.9" with < puts "1.10" first. Version and number-like text need to be split and compared as numbers.

Common mistake: Comparing dates stored as "27/10/2026" strings. Day-first strings do not sort in date order, so "01/12/2026" counts as smaller than "27/10/2026".

Interview tip: Mention localeCompare for user-facing text (it handles accents and case), and comparing Date objects or ISO strings for dates.
questions.codeSnippet:
console.log('10' < '9');        // true
console.log('10' < 9);          // false
console.log('Zebra' < 'apple'); // true
console.log(null >= 0);         // true
console.log(null == 0);         // false
console.log(['b', 'a', 'C'].sort((x, y) => x.localeCompare(y))); // ['a', 'b', 'C']

questions.question: Which of these values is falsy?
questions.answer:
Why C: The number 0 is one of the few falsy values.

Why not A: Any non-empty string is truthy, even the text "false".

Why not B: Every array is an object, and every object is truthy, even an empty one.

Why not D: A string with a space is not empty, so it is truthy.

questions.question: What does "5" + 3 return?
questions.answer:
Why B: With a string on one side, + joins the values as text, so you get "53".

Why not A: Numeric addition only happens when neither side is a string.

Why not C: Nothing fails here, so there is no NaN.

Why not D: The values are joined, not added and then turned into a string.

questions.question: What does "5" - 3 return?
questions.answer:
Why A: Minus only works on numbers, so "5" is converted to 5, and 5 - 3 is 2.

Why not B: Joining strings only happens with +.

Why not C: The result of subtraction is always a number, not a string.

Why not D: "5" converts cleanly to a number, so there is no NaN.

questions.question: What does NaN === NaN return?
questions.answer:
Why D: By the floating point rules NaN is not equal to anything, including itself.

Why not A: Object.is(NaN, NaN) would return true, but === does not.

Why not B: Comparisons never throw for NaN.

Why not C: === always returns a boolean.

questions.question: What does [] + {} evaluate to?
questions.answer:
Why B: [] becomes "" and {} becomes "[object Object]" when converted to strings, and + joins them.

Why not A: + only does math when neither side becomes a string.

Why not C: Arrays and objects are not converted to their source code text.

Why not D: There is no numeric conversion here, so NaN does not appear.

questions.question: What do null == 0 and null >= 0 return?
questions.answer:
Why C: == has a special rule: null only loosely equals undefined, so null == 0 is false. But >= converts null to the number 0, and 0 >= 0 is true.

Why not A: The >= comparison does convert null to 0, so it is true.

Why not B: Loose equality does not convert null to 0.

Why not D: The two results are the other way round.

questions.question: What is scope in JavaScript, and what kinds of scope are there?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Scope decides where a variable can be seen and used. JavaScript has global scope, function scope, block scope (for let and const) and module scope.

How it works:
Global: declared outside everything, visible everywhere
Function: variables inside a function are private to it
Block: let and const inside { } (if, for, while) stay in that block
Module: in ES modules, top-level variables are private to the file
Scope chain: if a variable is not found, JavaScript looks in the outer scope, then the next one out

Example: A helper variable total inside calculateBill() cannot be changed by other code, which prevents a different function from accidentally overwriting it.

Common mistake: Creating globals by accident, for example forgetting const in a sloppy-mode script. Two scripts using the same global name then overwrite each other.

Interview tip: Use the "rooms in a house" analogy: you can see out of your room into the hallway (outer scope), but people in the hallway cannot see into your room.

questions.question: What is hoisting in JavaScript?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Before code runs, JavaScript registers all declarations in their scope. Function declarations are fully hoisted (usable before their line), var is hoisted with the value undefined, and let, const and class are hoisted but cannot be used before their line.

How it works:
Function declaration: callable before it appears in the code
var: exists from the top of the function, but is undefined until assigned
let / const: exist but are in the temporal dead zone until their line
Function expression: follows the rules of its variable (var, let or const)
Class: like let, not usable before its line

Example: You can put the main logic at the top of a file and helper functions declared with function at the bottom. The calls at the top still work because of hoisting.

Common mistake: Thinking hoisting "moves code to the top". Nothing moves. The engine just sets up the variables before running the code line by line.

Interview tip: Show the three cases side by side (function, var, let) with what each prints. A small table like that is the clearest answer you can give.

questions.question: What is the temporal dead zone (TDZ)?
questions.answer:
Short answer: The TDZ is the time between the start of a scope and the line where a let, const or class variable is declared. Using the variable during that time throws a ReferenceError instead of giving undefined.

How it works:
Starts: when the block or function begins
Ends: when the declaration line runs
Inside the TDZ: reading or writing throws "Cannot access 'x' before initialization"
typeof: also throws in the TDZ, unlike for undeclared variables
Purpose: catch "used before set" bugs that var silently allowed

Example: Inside a function, a const config = loadConfig() line sits below code that already uses config. With var the code would run with undefined and fail somewhere confusing. With const it fails right away with a clear message.

Common mistake: Shadowing an outer variable, like const user = user.name inside a block. The inner user is in its TDZ while the right side runs, so it throws even though an outer user exists.

Interview tip: Say the TDZ is a feature: it turns silent bugs into loud errors. Then show the shadowing example, which is the trap most candidates miss.

questions.question: What is a closure? Explain it with an example.
questions.answer:
Short answer: A closure is a function that remembers the variables from the place where it was created, even after that outer function has finished. The inner function keeps a live link to those variables.

How it works:
Created: every time a function is created inside another function
Keeps: a reference to the outer variables, not a copy
Private state: outer code cannot touch those variables directly
Each call: calling the outer function again creates a new, separate closure

Example: makeCounter() returns a function. Each call of that function increases a count variable that only it can see. Two counters made by two calls of makeCounter() keep separate counts, like two separate tally counters in your hand.

Common mistake: Thinking the closure stores a snapshot of the value. It keeps the variable itself, so if the variable changes later, the closure sees the new value.

Interview tip: Give a real use, not only the counter: React hooks, event handlers and debounce all depend on closures. That shows you use the concept every day.

questions.question: What is the difference between a function declaration and a function expression, especially with hoisting?
questions.answer:
Short answer: A declaration (function name() {}) is hoisted completely, so you can call it before its line. An expression (const name = function () {} or an arrow function) is a value stored in a variable, so it follows that variable's hoisting rules.

How it works:
Declaration: function save() {}, usable anywhere in its scope
Expression with const or let: not usable before the line (TDZ)
Expression with var: the variable is undefined before the line, so calling it gives a TypeError
Named expression: const f = function inner() {}, inner is visible only inside itself

Example: An event handler file calls init() at the top. If init is a declaration it works. If someone refactors it to const init = () => {} at the bottom, the page breaks with "Cannot access 'init' before initialization".

Common mistake: Mixing both styles randomly in a codebase, so refactoring one function suddenly breaks call order somewhere else.

Interview tip: Mention that many teams prefer arrow function expressions for consistency and use declarations for top-level helpers. Either is fine if the team is consistent.

questions.question: What does lexical scope mean in JavaScript?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Lexical scope means a function's access to variables is decided by where the function is written in the code, not by where it is called from. The nesting of the source code decides the scope chain.

How it works:
Written inside: an inner function can use the variables of the functions around it
Called from elsewhere: the caller's local variables are not visible
Fixed at creation: the scope chain is set when the function is defined
this is different: this depends on how a function is called (except arrow functions)

Example: A logger function defined at the top of a module uses a level variable from the module. Calling logger() inside some other function that also has a level variable does not change which level the logger sees.

Common mistake: Expecting a callback to see variables from the function that calls it. It only sees variables from where the callback itself was written.

Interview tip: Contrast lexical scope with this. "Scope is decided where the function is written, this is decided where it is called (unless it is an arrow function)" is a crisp line interviewers remember.

questions.question: Why does a for loop with var and setTimeout print 3, 3, 3 instead of 0, 1, 2, and how do you fix it?
questions.answer:
Short answer: var creates one variable i for the whole function. All three callbacks close over that same i, and by the time they run the loop has finished and i is 3. let creates a new i for each loop run, so each callback gets its own value.

How it works:
var: one shared binding, final value 3
let: a fresh binding for every iteration
Callbacks run later: setTimeout callbacks run after the loop ends
Old fix: an IIFE that passes i as a parameter
Modern fix: just use let

Example: Attaching click handlers to buttons in a loop with var makes every button report "Button 3 clicked". Switching to let fixes all of them at once.

Common mistake: Thinking setTimeout(fn, 0) runs "immediately inside the loop". It always runs after the current code, so the loop always finishes first.

Interview tip: Explain both the cause (one shared variable) and the timing (callbacks run after the loop). Mentioning both shows you understand closures and the event loop together.
questions.codeSnippet:
for (var i = 0; i < 3; i++) setTimeout(() => console.log('var', i));  // 3 3 3
for (let j = 0; j < 3; j++) setTimeout(() => console.log('let', j));  // 0 1 2

questions.question: What are real-world uses of closures in JavaScript applications?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Closures give functions private memory. They power data privacy, function factories, once and memoize helpers, debounce, event handlers and React hooks.

How it works: Common uses:
Private state: a counter or cache that outside code cannot change
Factories: makeRateLimiter(10) returns a function with its own limit
once(): a function that runs only the first time
Memoize: keeps a cache of previous results
Debounce: remembers the timer id between calls
React: event handlers and effects see the props and state from their render

Example: A payment button wrapped in once(pay) cannot charge twice even if the user double-clicks, because the wrapper remembers "already called" in its closure.

Common mistake: Stale closures in React. A setInterval inside useEffect with an empty dependency array keeps the count value from the first render forever, so the counter stays at 1.

Interview tip: Mention the stale-closure bug and its fixes (functional updates like setCount(c => c + 1), or correct dependencies). It connects theory with a bug every React developer meets.

questions.question: Can closures cause memory leaks? Give an example and the fix.
questions.answer:
Short answer: Yes. A closure keeps its outer variables alive as long as the closure itself is reachable. If a long-living thing (a global listener, a timer, a cache) holds the closure, everything it references stays in memory too.

How it works:
Reachable: the garbage collector frees only what nothing points to
Long-living holders: window listeners, setInterval, global arrays, caches
What leaks: the outer variables, which may be large (data arrays, DOM nodes)
Fix: remove listeners, clear timers, limit cache size, avoid capturing big objects

Example: A component adds window.addEventListener('resize', handler) on every mount, and handler closes over a big list of 10,000 items. The listener is never removed, so after navigating back and forth 20 times, 20 lists stay in memory.

Common mistake: Thinking closures themselves are bad. The leak comes from keeping the closure reachable longer than needed, not from using closures.

Interview tip: Show the React fix: return a cleanup function from useEffect that removes the listener or clears the interval. It is short and very practical.

questions.question: What is an IIFE, why was it used, and is it still needed with ES modules?
questions.answer:
Short answer: An IIFE (Immediately Invoked Function Expression) is a function that runs right after it is created, like (function () { ... })(). It was used to create a private scope before JavaScript had modules and block scope.

How it works:
Syntax: wrap the function in parentheses, then call it with ()
Private scope: variables inside do not leak into the global scope
Module pattern: return an object with public methods, keep the rest private
Today: ES modules give each file its own scope, and let/const give block scope
Still useful: running async code at the top level in older setups, (async () => { ... })()

Example: Old jQuery plugins wrapped their code in an IIFE so their helper variables would not clash with other scripts on the same page.

Common mistake: Forgetting the semicolon on the line before an IIFE. The parentheses are then read as a function call on the previous line's value, causing a strange TypeError.

Interview tip: Say you rarely write IIFEs now, but you recognise them in older code and in bundler output. Understanding legacy code is valuable in real jobs.

questions.question: Which keyword declares a variable that is limited to the block { } it is declared in?
questions.answer:
Why B: let (and const) are block-scoped, so the variable exists only inside the nearest { }.

Why not A: var is function-scoped and ignores blocks like if and for.

Why not C: function declares a function, and function declarations in blocks have complicated legacy rules.

Why not D: global is not a JavaScript keyword.

questions.question: What does this code print? console.log(x); var x = 5;
questions.answer:
Why A: var x is hoisted and set to undefined, and the value 5 is assigned only when its line runs.

Why not B: The assignment has not happened yet when console.log runs.

Why not C: A ReferenceError would happen with let or const, not var.

Why not D: Hoisted var variables start as undefined, not null.

questions.question: What does this code do? console.log(y); let y = 5;
options: Throws ReferenceError: Cannot access 'y' before initialization
questions.correctAnswer: Throws ReferenceError: Cannot access 'y' before initialization
questions.answer:
Why D: y is in the temporal dead zone until its declaration line runs.

Why not A: Only var gives undefined before its line.

Why not B: The value is assigned later in the code.

Why not C: let variables are never set to null automatically.

questions.question: const add = makeAdder(10); where makeAdder = (x) => (y) => x + y. What does add(5) return?
questions.answer:
Why C: The returned function remembers x = 10 through a closure, so add(5) is 10 + 5.

Why not A: That ignores the remembered x.

Why not B: That ignores the new argument y.

Why not D: Both values are numbers, so the sum is a valid number.

questions.question: What does this print? for (let i = 0; i < 3; i++) setTimeout(() => console.log(i));
questions.answer:
Why B: let creates a new i for each iteration, and each callback closes over its own copy.

Why not A: That is the result with var, which shares one i.

Why not C: Each iteration gets a different value, not the first one.

Why not D: i is defined and in scope for every callback.

questions.question: What happens here? sayHi(); var sayHi = function () { console.log("hi"); };
options: TypeError: sayHi is not a function
questions.correctAnswer: TypeError: sayHi is not a function
questions.answer:
Why C: var sayHi is hoisted as undefined, so the code tries to call undefined, which is a TypeError.

Why not A: Only function declarations are callable before their line.

Why not B: The variable exists (hoisted), so it is not a ReferenceError.

Why not D: Calling undefined throws, it does not print anything.

questions.question: What are the differences between arrow functions and regular functions?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Arrow functions are shorter and do not have their own this, arguments, super or new.target. They take this from the surrounding code. Regular functions get this from how they are called and can be used as constructors.

How it works:
this: arrow takes it from outside, regular depends on the call
arguments: arrow has none, use rest parameters (...args)
new: arrow functions cannot be used with new
Short return: (x) => x * 2 returns without the return keyword
Methods: regular (or shorthand) functions are better for object methods

Example: Inside a class method, setTimeout(() => this.save(), 1000) works because the arrow keeps the method's this. A regular function there would lose this.

Common mistake: Using an arrow function as an object method, like { name: 'Ali', greet: () => this.name }. this is not the object, so greet returns undefined.

Interview tip: Sum it up as "arrow functions for callbacks, regular or shorthand methods for object methods". It is the practical rule most teams follow.

questions.question: How does JavaScript decide what this refers to inside a function?
questions.answer:
Short answer: For regular functions, this depends on how the function is called, not where it is written. There are four rules, checked in order: new, explicit binding, method call, and default. Arrow functions skip the rules and use the outer this.

How it works:
new binding: new User() makes this the new object
Explicit: fn.call(obj), fn.apply(obj) or fn.bind(obj) set this to obj
Implicit (method): obj.fn() makes this obj, the thing before the dot
Default: plain fn() gives undefined in strict mode (the global object in sloppy mode)
Arrow function: this comes from the surrounding scope

Example: button.addEventListener('click', handler) calls handler with this set to the button, because the browser calls it like a method of the element.

Common mistake: Thinking this means "the object where the function was defined". A method copied into a variable and called alone loses its object.

Interview tip: Say "look at the call site" and walk through the four rules. It is the clearest way to answer any this puzzle on the spot.

questions.question: What is the difference between call, apply and bind?
questions.answer:
Short answer: All three set this for a function. call and apply run the function immediately: call takes arguments one by one, apply takes them as an array. bind does not run it, it returns a new function with this fixed for later.

How it works:
call: fn.call(thisArg, a, b)
apply: fn.apply(thisArg, [a, b])
bind: const bound = fn.bind(thisArg, a), then bound(b)
Partial application: bind can also fix the first arguments
Bound functions: cannot be re-bound to another this

Example: In older React class components, this.handleClick = this.handleClick.bind(this) in the constructor made the handler keep the component as this when passed to onClick.

Common mistake: Using bind when you meant call, like fn.bind(obj) and expecting it to run. Nothing happens because bind only returns a function.

Interview tip: Remember it as "Call for Commas, Apply for Arrays, Bind for Later". Interviewers like a short memory hook plus a real use.

questions.question: What are higher-order functions and callbacks in JavaScript?
questions.answer:
Short answer: A higher-order function takes a function as an argument, returns a function, or both. The function you pass in is a callback. They let you reuse logic and customise behaviour.

How it works:
Take a function: map, filter, sort, addEventListener, setTimeout
Return a function: debounce(fn), makeMultiplier(2), middleware factories
Why: separate "what to do" from "how to loop or when to run"
First-class functions: functions are values, so they can be stored and passed around

Example: An Express role check, allowRoles('admin'), is a higher-order function: it takes settings and returns a middleware function that runs later for each request.

Common mistake: Calling the callback instead of passing it, like button.addEventListener('click', save()). save runs immediately once, and its return value (usually undefined) is passed as the handler.

Interview tip: Mention that React components with render props or custom hooks follow the same idea. Showing the link between basic JavaScript and frameworks is a strong signal.

questions.question: How do default parameters, rest parameters and the arguments object work?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Default parameters give a value when an argument is undefined. Rest parameters (...args) collect the remaining arguments into a real array. The old arguments object is array-like, exists only in regular functions, and is rarely needed now.

How it works:
Default: function greet(name = 'Guest'), used only for undefined, not for null
Rest: function sum(...nums), always a real array
arguments: array-like, no map or filter, not in arrow functions
Order: rest must be the last parameter
length: counts parameters before the first default or rest

Example: A logger function log(level = 'info', ...messages) can be called as log(undefined, 'Server', 'started') and still uses "info", with messages as an array.

Common mistake: Passing null to use the default, like greet(null). null is a real value, so name becomes null and the page shows "Hi null".

Interview tip: Mention that rest parameters replaced most uses of arguments, and that default parameters can use earlier parameters, like function f(a, b = a * 2).

questions.question: What is currying, and how is it useful in real code?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Currying turns a function that takes several arguments into a chain of functions that each take one, like add(a)(b) instead of add(a, b). It makes it easy to create specialised versions of a general function.

How it works:
Curried: const add = (a) => (b) => a + b
Specialise: const add10 = add(10), then add10(5) is 15
Partial application: fixing some arguments, which bind can also do
Relies on closures: each step remembers the earlier arguments

Example: A logging helper const log = (level) => (module) => (msg) => ... lets you create const authError = log('error')('auth') once and call authError('Bad token') everywhere in the auth code.

Common mistake: Currying everything "because it is functional". Deeply curried code with many small arrows is hard to read for teammates who are not used to the style.

Interview tip: Interviewers often ask you to write a generic curry(fn) helper. Mention that it uses fn.length to know when enough arguments have been collected.

questions.question: Why does this become undefined when you pass an object method as a callback, and how do you fix it?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Passing obj.method gives only the function, without the object. When it is called later as a plain function, this follows the default rule (undefined in strict mode). Fix it with an arrow wrapper, bind, or class arrow fields.

How it works:
Passing: setTimeout(user.logout, 1000) passes just the function
Later call: called as logout(), not user.logout()
Fix 1: setTimeout(() => user.logout(), 1000)
Fix 2: setTimeout(user.logout.bind(user), 1000)
Fix 3: class field logout = () => { ... } keeps this per instance

Example: A Timer class passes this.tick to setInterval. tick runs, this is not the timer, and this.seconds++ throws "Cannot read properties of undefined (reading 'seconds')".

Common mistake: Adding .bind(this) inside render or JSX for every element. It creates a new function on every render, which can break memoized child components.

Interview tip: Explain why (the call site lost the object) before giving fixes. Showing the cause first is what separates a strong answer from a memorized one.

questions.question: What is a pure function, and why do pure functions matter in React and testing?
questions.answer:
Short answer: A pure function always returns the same output for the same input and has no side effects: it does not change outside variables, the DOM, the network or its arguments. Pure functions are predictable, easy to test and safe to cache.

How it works:
Same input, same output: no dependency on time, randomness or global state
No side effects: no mutation, no API calls, no console or DOM changes
Benefits: easy unit tests, safe memoization, easier debugging
React: components and reducers should be pure during render
Side effects: belong in event handlers and useEffect

Example: A calculateTotal(items) function that only reads items and returns a number can be tested with 5 lines and reused on the server. A version that also writes to localStorage and changes items in place is hard to test and causes surprising bugs.

Common mistake: Sorting an array prop with props.items.sort() inside a component. sort mutates the original array, so the parent's data changes during render.

Interview tip: Mention that React Strict Mode renders components twice in development to catch impure render logic. It is a concrete fact that shows real React experience.

questions.question: What is function composition, and how would you write a pipe() helper?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Composition builds a new function by chaining small functions, where each one's output becomes the next one's input. pipe(f, g, h)(x) means h(g(f(x))), reading left to right.

How it works:
Small functions: each does one clear step
pipe: runs left to right, easy to read like a recipe
compose: runs right to left, common in math and some libraries
Implementation: reduce over the list of functions
Requirement: each function takes one input and returns one output

Example: Cleaning a username: pipe(trim, toLowerCase, removeSpaces)(input). Each step is tiny and testable, and adding a new step is one word.

Common mistake: Putting a function that returns a Promise in the middle of a normal pipe. The next function gets a Promise instead of a value. Async pipelines need an async version that awaits each step.

Interview tip: Write pipe with reduce in one line during the interview. It shows comfort with higher-order functions and reduce at the same time.

questions.question: What happens step by step when you call a function with the new keyword?
questions.answer:
Short answer: new creates an empty object, links it to the function's prototype, runs the function with this set to that object, and returns the object (unless the function returns a different object).

How it works:
Step 1: create a new empty object
Step 2: set its prototype to Constructor.prototype
Step 3: call the constructor with this pointing to the new object
Step 4: if the constructor returns an object, use that, otherwise return the new object
Classes: work the same way underneath

Example: new User('Ali') creates { name: 'Ali' } whose prototype has the shared greet method, so a thousand users share one greet function instead of a thousand copies.

Common mistake: Forgetting new with an old-style constructor, like const u = User('Ali'). this is undefined (strict) or the global object (sloppy), so it throws or creates global variables. Classes throw a clear error if called without new.

Interview tip: Interviewers sometimes ask you to write your own myNew(). Show it with Object.create and apply, it proves you understand prototypes too.

questions.question: Which kind of function does NOT have its own this?
options: An object method written as greet() { }
questions.answer:
Why A: Arrow functions take this from the surrounding scope instead of creating their own.

Why not B: Function declarations get this from how they are called.

Why not C: Shorthand methods get this from the object they are called on.

Why not D: Class methods also get this from the call, usually the instance.

questions.question: In strict mode: const obj = { name: "A", greet() { return this.name; } }; const g = obj.greet; g(); What happens?
options: Throws a TypeError because this is undefined
questions.correctAnswer: Throws a TypeError because this is undefined
questions.answer:
Why D: g() is a plain call, so this is undefined in strict mode, and reading undefined.name throws.

Why not A: The connection to obj is lost when the method is stored in g.

Why not B: this itself is undefined, so reading a property of it throws instead of returning undefined.

Why not C: In sloppy mode in a browser it could read window.name (often ""), but not in strict mode.

questions.question: Which method calls a function with a given this and passes the arguments as an array?
questions.answer:
Why C: apply takes this and an array of arguments, and runs the function immediately.

Why not A: call takes the arguments one by one, separated by commas.

Why not B: bind does not run the function, it returns a new one.

Why not D: Functions have no invoke method in JavaScript.

questions.question: What does fn.bind(obj) return?
options: The result of calling fn with this as obj
A new function that always runs with this set to obj
obj with fn added as a method
questions.correctAnswer: A new function that always runs with this set to obj
questions.answer:
Why B: bind creates a new function with this fixed, to be called later.

Why not A: That is what call and apply do.

Why not C: bind does not change obj.

Why not D: bind always returns a function.

questions.question: What does obj.f() return? const obj = { n: 1, f() { return [1].map(() => this.n); } };
questions.answer:
Why A: The arrow function inside map takes this from f, and f was called as obj.f(), so this.n is 1.

Why not B: That would happen with a regular function callback, which loses this.

Why not C: this is obj, so reading n works fine.

Why not D: No math happens, so NaN cannot appear.

questions.question: What is the value of f.length for function f(a, b = 2, ...rest) {}?
questions.answer:
Why D: length counts only the parameters before the first default value or rest parameter, so only a.

Why not A: The rest parameter is never counted.

Why not B: b has a default value, so counting stops before it.

Why not C: a has no default, so it is counted.

questions.question: What are the different ways to create an object in JavaScript?
questions.answer:
Short answer: The common ways are an object literal { }, a class or constructor function with new, Object.create(proto), and factory functions that return a literal. Literals are used most of the time.

How it works:
Literal: const user = { name: 'Ali' }, simple and fast
Class / constructor: new User('Ali'), many objects sharing methods
Object.create(proto): choose the prototype directly, or null for none
Factory function: createUser('Ali') returns a literal, no new or this needed
From entries: Object.fromEntries([['a', 1]])

Example: API responses are plain literals. A game with 500 enemies uses a class, so all enemies share the same attack method through the prototype instead of 500 copies.

Common mistake: Using new Object() or new Array() out of habit. Literals are shorter and avoid surprises like new Array(3) creating 3 empty slots instead of [3].

Interview tip: Mention when you would pick each one. Choosing based on the situation shows judgement, not just syntax knowledge.

questions.question: What is the prototype chain in JavaScript?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Every object has a hidden link to another object called its prototype. When you read a property that the object does not have, JavaScript looks at its prototype, then that prototype's prototype, until it finds the property or reaches null.

How it works:
Own properties: stored directly on the object
Lookup: if missing, check the prototype, then the next one up
End: Object.prototype, whose prototype is null
Shared methods: arrays get map and filter from Array.prototype
Writing: assigning a property always creates it on the object itself

Example: [1, 2].map works even though your array has no map property. The lookup goes from the array to Array.prototype, finds map and calls it with this as your array.

Common mistake: Adding methods to built-in prototypes, like Array.prototype.last = ... . It can clash with future JavaScript features and other libraries (this happened with real methods like flatten and contains).

Interview tip: Draw the chain: myArray, then Array.prototype, then Object.prototype, then null. A quick diagram explains inheritance better than any definition.
questions.codeSnippet:
const arr = [1, 2];
console.log(Object.getPrototypeOf(arr) === Array.prototype);            // true
console.log(Object.getPrototypeOf(Array.prototype) === Object.prototype); // true
console.log(Object.getPrototypeOf(Object.prototype));                     // null
console.log(arr.hasOwnProperty('map'));                                    // false

questions.question: What is the difference between a shallow copy and a deep copy, and how do you make each?
questions.answer:
Short answer: A shallow copy creates a new top-level object, but nested objects are still shared. A deep copy copies everything, so nested objects are separate too.

How it works:
Shallow: { ...obj }, Object.assign({}, obj), [...arr], arr.slice()
Deep (modern): structuredClone(obj), keeps Dates, Maps, Sets and circular references
Deep (old trick): JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(obj)), loses Dates, undefined, functions, Map and Set
Libraries: lodash cloneDeep for special cases

Example: A React form copies state with { ...form } and then changes form.address.city. The original state's address also changes, because the nested address object was shared. structuredClone, or spreading the nested level too, fixes it.

Common mistake: Using the JSON trick on objects with dates. After the copy, createdAt is a string, not a Date, so createdAt.getTime() crashes.

Interview tip: Mention that structuredClone cannot copy functions or DOM nodes, so for class instances you may need your own clone method.

questions.question: What is the difference between Object.keys(), Object.entries() and a for...in loop?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Object.keys, values and entries return only the object's own enumerable string keys as arrays. for...in also visits enumerable keys inherited from the prototype chain, which can give surprising extra keys.

How it works:
Object.keys(obj): ['a', 'b']
Object.values(obj): [1, 2]
Object.entries(obj): [['a', 1], ['b', 2]], great with for...of and destructuring
for...in: own plus inherited enumerable keys
Order: integer-like keys first in ascending order, then other strings in insertion order

Example: Turning a settings object into a list of form rows: Object.entries(settings).map(([key, value]) => ...). It is clear and skips anything inherited.

Common mistake: Expecting keys to keep insertion order when they look like numbers. { b: 1, 2: 'x', 1: 'y' } gives the keys ['1', '2', 'b'].

Interview tip: Mention Object.fromEntries for the reverse direction, for example filtering an object: Object.fromEntries(Object.entries(obj).filter(...)).

questions.question: What is the difference between Object.freeze(), Object.seal() and Object.preventExtensions()?
questions.answer:
Short answer: They are three levels of locking. preventExtensions blocks new properties. seal also blocks deleting. freeze also blocks changing values. All three are shallow.

How it works:
preventExtensions: no new properties, can delete and change
seal: no new, no delete, can still change existing values
freeze: no new, no delete, no change
Checks: Object.isExtensible, Object.isSealed, Object.isFrozen
Errors: silent in sloppy mode, TypeError in strict mode

Example: A constants object of order statuses is frozen so no code can change "PAID" by mistake. A settings object is sealed so the shape stays fixed but users can still change the values.

Common mistake: Expecting freeze to protect nested data. order.items.push(x) still works on a frozen order.

Interview tip: A neat way to remember: each level adds one more lock. Then mention that in strict mode (ES modules) the violations throw, which helps catch bugs.

questions.question: What is the difference between __proto__, Object.getPrototypeOf() and a function's prototype property?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Every object has an internal prototype link, which you read with Object.getPrototypeOf(obj) (or the old __proto__ accessor). A function's prototype property is different: it is the object that becomes the prototype of instances created with new.

How it works:
obj.__proto__: old accessor for the link, avoid in new code
Object.getPrototypeOf(obj): the modern way to read the link
Object.setPrototypeOf(obj, p): changes it, slow, avoid in hot code
Fn.prototype: only on functions and classes, used by new
Connection: Object.getPrototypeOf(new Fn()) === Fn.prototype

Example: For class User, every user object's prototype is User.prototype, which holds the methods. User itself (the function) has Function.prototype as its own prototype.

Common mistake: Writing user.prototype.greet. Instances do not have a prototype property, only constructor functions and classes do, so it is undefined and throws.

Interview tip: Say "prototype is a property of constructors, the prototype link is a property of every object". This one sentence clears the confusion interviewers are testing for.

questions.question: What are property descriptors, getters and setters, and when would you use Object.defineProperty?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Every property has hidden settings called a descriptor: value, writable, enumerable and configurable (or get and set for accessors). Object.defineProperty lets you control them, for example to make a read-only or hidden property, or a computed one.

How it works:
writable: false means the value cannot change
enumerable: false hides it from Object.keys, for...in and JSON.stringify
configurable: false blocks deleting it or changing its settings
get / set: run a function when the property is read or written
Defaults: defineProperty sets missing flags to false, unlike normal assignment

Example: A User model defines fullName with a getter that joins first and last name, and an id that is non-writable, so code like user.id = 5 has no effect.

Common mistake: Using defineProperty and forgetting that enumerable defaults to false. The property then vanishes from JSON responses and the API seems to "lose" a field.

Interview tip: Mention that Vue 2's reactivity was built on defineProperty getters and setters, and Vue 3 switched to Proxy. It connects the concept to real frameworks.

questions.question: Why is { a: 1 } === { a: 1 } false, and how do you compare two objects by their content?
questions.answer:
Short answer: === compares object references, and two literals create two different objects. To compare content, you need a deep-equal function that compares keys and values recursively, or a library helper.

How it works:
Reference check: true only for the very same object
JSON.stringify compare: quick, but key order matters and it skips undefined and functions
Deep equal: same key set, then compare each value recursively
Libraries: lodash isEqual, or Node's util.isDeepStrictEqual on the server
Arrays: same idea, same length and same items in order

Example: A "Save" button should be enabled only when the form differs from the original data. Comparing with === always says "changed", while a deep-equal check enables it only on real edits.

Common mistake: Using JSON.stringify(a) === JSON.stringify(b) and getting false for { a: 1, b: 2 } vs { b: 2, a: 1 } just because the key order differs.

Interview tip: Interviewers may ask you to write deepEqual. Mention handling null, arrays vs objects, different key counts, and (as an extra) Dates and circular references.

questions.question: How does inheritance work with prototypes without using class, and why should you avoid changing prototypes at runtime?
questions.answer:
Short answer: You can link objects directly with Object.create(parent), so the child inherits parent's properties through the prototype chain. Changing an object's prototype later with setPrototypeOf, or extending built-ins, hurts performance and causes conflicts.

How it works:
Object.create(proto): new object whose prototype is proto
Delegation: missing properties are looked up on the parent
Classes: the same mechanism with nicer syntax
setPrototypeOf after creation: engines de-optimise these objects
Built-ins: adding to Array.prototype can clash with future standard methods

Example: const admin = Object.create(user); admin.role = 'admin'. admin.greet() uses user's greet, and changing user.greet later changes it for admin too, because it is shared, not copied.

Common mistake: Thinking Object.create copies the parent's properties. Nothing is copied, the child only points to the parent, so changes to the parent show up in the child.

Interview tip: Mention the MooTools story: it added Array.prototype.flatten, so the standard had to name the new method flat instead. That example explains why extending built-ins is risky.

questions.question: How does JSON.stringify handle undefined, functions, NaN, Dates, Maps and circular references?
questions.answer:
Short answer: JSON only supports strings, numbers, booleans, null, arrays and plain objects. Other values are dropped, changed to null, converted with toJSON, turned into {}, or cause an error.

How it works:
undefined, functions, symbols: dropped from objects, become null inside arrays
NaN and Infinity: become null
Date: converted with toJSON to an ISO string
Map and Set: become {} because their data is not in normal properties
BigInt: throws a TypeError
Circular reference: throws "Converting circular structure to JSON"
Replacer and toJSON: let you control the output

Example: An API sends { lastLogin: new Date() }. The client receives a string, and code that calls lastLogin.getTime() breaks until it does new Date(lastLogin) first.

Common mistake: Returning a Map from an Express route with res.json(). The client gets {} and the data seems to have disappeared.

Interview tip: Mention converting Maps with Object.fromEntries(map) before sending, and using a reviver in JSON.parse to turn date strings back into Dates.

questions.question: What does {} === {} return?
questions.answer:
Why A: Each {} creates a new object, and === compares references, so two different objects are never strictly equal.

Why not B: They look the same, but they are two separate objects in memory.

Why not C: Comparisons always return a boolean.

Why not D: Comparing objects is always allowed.

questions.question: const a = { x: { y: 1 } }; const b = { ...a }; b.x.y = 2; What is a.x.y?
questions.answer:
Why C: Spread makes a shallow copy. b.x and a.x point to the same nested object, so the change shows in both.

Why not A: That would need a deep copy, like structuredClone(a).

Why not B: The nested property still exists.

Why not D: Changing a nested property is allowed.

questions.question: In strict mode, what happens when you assign a new value to a property of a frozen object?
questions.answer:
Why D: Strict mode turns writes to read-only properties into errors: "Cannot assign to read only property".

Why not A: Freezing makes the properties read-only.

Why not B: That is what happens in sloppy (non-strict) mode.

Why not C: A frozen object can never be unfrozen.

questions.question: What is the main difference between for...in and Object.keys() for an object?
options: for...in also visits enumerable keys inherited from the prototype chain
questions.correctAnswer: for...in also visits enumerable keys inherited from the prototype chain
questions.answer:
Why B: for...in walks the prototype chain too, while Object.keys returns only the object's own keys.

Why not A: for...in is meant for objects, and using it on arrays is discouraged.

Why not C: Object.keys returns own keys only.

Why not D: Inherited keys are the important difference.

questions.question: What does JSON.stringify({ a: undefined, b: () => 1, c: NaN }) return?
questions.answer:
Why C: undefined and functions are dropped from objects, and NaN is not valid JSON, so it becomes null.

Why not A: Inside objects, undefined and functions are removed, not turned into null.

Why not B: undefined and NaN are not valid JSON values, so they never appear as written.

Why not D: Only BigInt values and circular references throw.

questions.question: const o = Object.create(null); What does "toString" in o return?
questions.answer:
Why B: Object.create(null) makes an object with no prototype, so it does not inherit toString from Object.prototype.

Why not A: Normal objects inherit toString, but this one has no prototype.

Why not C: The in operator works on any object, including prototype-less ones.

Why not D: in always returns true or false.

questions.question: What is a class in JavaScript, and is it different from a constructor function?
questions.answer:
Short answer: A class is a cleaner syntax for creating objects that share methods. Underneath it still uses functions and prototypes, but it adds useful rules: you must call it with new, the body is in strict mode, and methods are not enumerable.

How it works:
constructor(): runs when you call new, sets up the instance
Methods: written in the class body, stored once on the prototype
Fields: name = 'x' declares per-instance properties
Rules: calling without new throws, class body is strict mode
typeof: typeof MyClass is "function"

Example: class Course { constructor(title) { this.title = title; } publish() { ... } } lets you create 100 courses that all share one publish method.

Common mistake: Saying JavaScript classes work like Java classes. There are no real "class objects" being copied, objects still delegate to a prototype at runtime.

Interview tip: Say "classes are syntax sugar over prototypes, with a few safety rules added". Then show that typeof a class is "function". It shows you know what happens underneath.

questions.question: How do extends and super work in JavaScript classes?
questions.answer:
Short answer: extends makes one class inherit from another. Inside the child, super(...) calls the parent constructor, and super.method() calls the parent's version of a method. In a child constructor you must call super() before using this.

How it works:
extends: sets the child prototype to inherit from the parent prototype
super(args): runs the parent constructor, required before this
super.method(): reuse the parent logic, then add more
Static inheritance: static methods are inherited too
Built-ins: you can extend Error, Array and others

Example: class AppError extends Error { constructor(message, status) { super(message); this.status = status; } } gives you a real Error with a stack trace plus an HTTP status for your API.

Common mistake: Using this before super() in the child constructor. JavaScript throws "Must call super constructor in derived class before accessing 'this'".

Interview tip: The AppError example is the best one to give, because it is real, short and shows inheritance from a built-in.

questions.question: What are static methods and properties in a class, and when should you use them?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Static members belong to the class itself, not to instances. Call them as ClassName.method(). Use them for helpers and factories that do not need a specific object.

How it works:
static method: ClassName.create(...), not on instances
static field: shared constants or counters on the class
this inside static: refers to the class, so subclasses can reuse it
Not on instances: instance.staticMethod is undefined

Example: User.fromJSON(data) builds a User from API data, and Temperature.fromFahrenheit(98) creates a Temperature from a different unit. Mongoose's Model.find() is also a static method.

Common mistake: Making everything static, which turns the class into a bag of functions. If no method uses this or instances, a plain module with functions is simpler.

Interview tip: Mention the factory pattern: static methods that create instances in different ways are a clean replacement for a constructor with many optional parameters.

questions.question: How do private class fields (#) work, and how are they different from the _underscore convention?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Fields starting with # are truly private: only code inside the class body can read or write them, and the engine enforces it. An underscore like _balance is just a naming hint, and anyone can still change it.

How it works:
#field: declared in the class body, used as this.#field
Outside access: obj.#field is a SyntaxError, the code does not even run
Private methods: #validate() works the same way
Check: #field in obj tells if an object has that private field
Not in JSON or Object.keys: private fields are invisible from outside

Example: A BankAccount with #balance and a deposit() method makes sure the balance only changes through validated methods. With _balance, any code could write account._balance = 1000000.

Common mistake: Using the same # name in a subclass and expecting it to share the parent's field. Private fields are per class, the child cannot see the parent's #fields.

Interview tip: Mention closures as the older way to get privacy, and that # fields are now supported in all modern browsers and Node.

questions.question: How do getters and setters work in JavaScript classes, and what are they good for?
questions.answer:
Short answer: A getter (get name()) runs a function when a property is read. A setter (set name(v)) runs when it is written. They let you compute values or validate input while keeping simple property syntax.

How it works:
get: computed value, like fullName from first and last
set: validation or conversion, like trimming and checking an email
Backing field: usually a private #field holds the real value
Read-only: a getter without a setter cannot be assigned (throws in strict mode)

Example: A Product class has get priceLabel() that returns "Rs 1,500" and set price(v) that rejects negative numbers. Code using it just writes product.price = 1500.

Common mistake: A setter that assigns to the same property name, like set name(v) { this.name = v; }. It calls itself forever and crashes with "Maximum call stack size exceeded".

Interview tip: Mention that getters should be cheap and free of side effects, since people expect reading a property to be fast and safe.

questions.question: Explain the four pillars of OOP with JavaScript examples.
questions.answer:
Short answer: Encapsulation hides internal data, inheritance reuses code from a parent, polymorphism lets different objects respond to the same method in their own way, and abstraction exposes only a simple interface.

How it works:
Encapsulation: #balance can only change through deposit()
Inheritance: class Admin extends User
Polymorphism: shape.area() works for Circle and Square, each with its own formula
Abstraction: a sendEmail(user) method hides SMTP details

Example: A notifications system has EmailNotifier, SmsNotifier and PushNotifier, all with a send(message) method. The code loops over notifiers and calls send() without caring which type each one is. That is polymorphism in a real feature.

Common mistake: Giving only textbook definitions. Interviewers want a small example that shows each idea in code.

Interview tip: Use one connected example (like the notifiers) to show several pillars at once. It is easier to follow and shows you can apply the ideas, not just recite them.

questions.question: What does "favor composition over inheritance" mean, and how do you apply it in JavaScript?
questions.answer:
