Short answer: Instead of building deep class trees, build objects from small, focused pieces of behaviour. Inheritance says "is a", composition says "has a" or "can do". Composition is more flexible and avoids fragile hierarchies.

How it works:
Inheritance problem: deep trees break when a parent changes, and some children inherit features they should not have
Composition: combine small functions or objects, like canFly and canSwim
Mixins: copy methods from several sources with Object.assign
In React: components are composed from smaller components and hooks, not inherited

Example: A game has Duck, Fish and Plane. Inheritance struggles because Duck both flies and swims. With composition, each object gets exactly the abilities it needs: duck = { ...canFly(state), ...canSwim(state) }.

Common mistake: Creating a BaseController, then BaseApiController, then BaseAuthApiController just to share a few helpers. Small helper functions or middleware are simpler.

Interview tip: Mention that React itself recommends composition over inheritance for components. It is a strong, real-world reference.

questions.question: What is the trade-off between class methods and arrow function class fields for keeping this?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Arrow function fields (handle = () => {}) keep this bound to the instance automatically, which is handy for callbacks. But they create a new function for every instance, and they are not on the prototype, so subclasses cannot use super.handle().

How it works:
Prototype method: one shared function, needs binding when passed as a callback
Arrow field: one function per instance, this is always the instance
Memory: 10,000 instances means 10,000 copies of each arrow field
Inheritance: arrow fields cannot be called with super, and overriding works differently
Testing: prototype methods are easier to spy on

Example: In a class-based React component, handleClick = () => { this.setState(...) } avoids writing bind in the constructor, which is why it became popular.

Common mistake: Making every method an arrow field "just in case". For objects created in large numbers, it wastes memory, and it breaks subclass patterns.

Interview tip: Say you use arrow fields only for methods passed as callbacks, and normal methods for everything else. A balanced answer shows real understanding.

questions.question: Are classes hoisted in JavaScript, and what other rules make classes different from functions?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Class declarations are hoisted like let: the name exists, but using it before the declaration throws a ReferenceError (temporal dead zone). Classes also run in strict mode, must be called with new, and their methods are not enumerable.

How it works:
Hoisting: new User() before class User {} throws
Strict mode: always on inside class bodies
Calling: User() without new throws a TypeError
Methods: non-enumerable, so they do not show up in for...in
Class expressions: const User = class { }, follows the variable's rules

Example: Moving a helper class to the bottom of a file, below the code that creates instances, breaks the app with "Cannot access 'User' before initialization". The same move works for function declarations.

Common mistake: Assuming classes work like function declarations, because typeof says "function".

Interview tip: Compare the three: function declarations are fully hoisted, var is hoisted as undefined, let, const and class are hoisted into the TDZ. One clear comparison is a great answer.

questions.question: How does instanceof work, and when can it give surprising results?
questions.answer:
Short answer: a instanceof B checks whether B.prototype appears anywhere in a's prototype chain. It does not look at how the object was built or what properties it has, so it can be fooled or fail in a few situations.

How it works:
Check: walks a's prototype chain looking for B.prototype
Primitives: 'text' instanceof String is false
Changed prototypes: Object.setPrototypeOf can make it true or false
Other realms: an array from an iframe fails instanceof Array, use Array.isArray
Custom: Symbol.hasInstance can change the result

Example: In an Express error handler, err instanceof AppError tells your own errors apart from library errors. If two copies of your package are installed (different versions), the check can fail because there are two different AppError classes.

Common mistake: Using instanceof to check plain data from JSON. Parsed objects are plain objects, so data instanceof User is always false, even if it has all the user fields.

Interview tip: Mention duck typing as the alternative: check for the methods or fields you need. For errors, an err.name or err.code check survives duplicate packages.

questions.question: Which design patterns have you used in JavaScript? Explain Module, Singleton, Factory and Observer with examples.
questions.answer:
Short answer: A design pattern is a named, reusable solution to a common design problem. In JavaScript and Node.js the ones you meet most are Module, Singleton, Factory and Observer.

How it works:
Module: keep data private and export only a small public API (ES modules or a closure)
Singleton: one shared instance, like a database connection; Node caches modules, so exporting one instance gives a singleton
Factory: a function that decides which object to create, so callers do not use new and if/else everywhere
Observer: listeners subscribe to an event and get notified (EventEmitter, addEventListener)

Example: In a MERN app the Mongoose connection file is a singleton, a createNotifier("email") factory returns the right sender, and an "order created" EventEmitter (observer) triggers the email.

Common mistake: Listing pattern names with no real example, or using Singleton everywhere. Hidden global state makes code hard to test.

Interview tip: Pick two patterns you actually used in your own project and explain the problem each one solved.

questions.question: Does JavaScript support method overloading and method overriding? How do you get the same effect?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Overriding: yes. A child class method with the same name replaces the parent one, and super.method() can still call the parent. Overloading: no. A second method with the same name silently replaces the first, so you handle different arguments inside one function.

How it works:
Overriding: lookup walks the prototype chain and finds the child method first
super.method(): calls the parent version from inside the override
Overloading: JavaScript keeps only one function per name
Same effect: check argument count or type, use default parameters, rest parameters or one options object

Example: Shape.area() returns 0 and Circle overrides area() with its own formula. A greet(name, options) function accepts one name or an array of names instead of two "overloads".

Common mistake: Writing two methods with the same name in a class and expecting both to work. Only the last one survives, and there is no error.

Interview tip: Mention that TypeScript allows overload signatures for type checking, but it still compiles to one JavaScript function.

questions.question: What is the diamond problem in multiple inheritance, and how does JavaScript avoid it?
questions.answer:
Short answer: If class D inherits from both B and C, and both override a method from A, D does not know which version to use. JavaScript avoids this because a class can extend only one class: every object has a single prototype chain. To reuse behaviour from several places you use mixins or composition, and you choose the order yourself.

How it works:
One prototype: each object has exactly one [[Prototype]], so method lookup follows one line
extends: only one parent class is allowed
Mixins: functions that take a class and return an extended class; the last one applied wins
Composition: keep helper objects as properties instead of inheriting from them

Example: A Duck gets CanFly and CanSwim mixins. Both define move(), and the mixin applied last decides the result, so there is no ambiguity.

Common mistake: Claiming JavaScript has multiple inheritance because of mixins. Mixins still build one single chain.

Interview tip: Mention how other languages solve it: C++ has virtual inheritance, and Java and C# allow many interfaces but only one parent class.

questions.question: What are the SOLID principles? Give a JavaScript or Node.js example for each.
questions.answer:
Short answer: SOLID is five design rules that keep code easy to change: Single responsibility, Open/closed, Liskov substitution, Interface segregation and Dependency inversion.

How it works:
S: one reason to change; the controller handles HTTP, the service handles business rules
O: add behaviour by adding code, not editing old code (a new payment gateway object)
L: a child must work wherever the parent works (a Square that breaks setWidth breaks this rule)
I: do not force code to depend on methods it does not use; keep objects small and focused
D: depend on abstractions; pass the gateway or repository into the service instead of requiring it inside

Example: OrderService receives a payment gateway in its constructor. JazzCash and Stripe gateways both have charge(), so adding a new one needs no change to OrderService (O and D together).

Common mistake: Reciting the five definitions without code, or forcing all five onto a tiny script where they only add layers.

Interview tip: Show one small example that covers two or three letters, then explain the rest briefly. Dependency injection also makes testing with fakes easy.

questions.question: Which keyword makes one class inherit from another?
questions.answer:
Why C: class Child extends Parent sets up inheritance between the two classes.

Why not A: inherits is not a JavaScript keyword (Node once had a util.inherits helper).

Why not B: implements exists in TypeScript and Java, not in JavaScript classes.

Why not D: super calls the parent, but it does not create the inheritance.

questions.question: A child class constructor uses this before calling super(). What happens?
options: this refers to the parent object
this is undefined but no error is thrown
questions.answer:
Why D: In a derived class, this does not exist until super() has run, so accessing it throws a ReferenceError.

Why not A: There is no separate parent object, super() creates the instance.

Why not B: super() is only automatic when you write no constructor at all.

Why not C: JavaScript throws instead of giving undefined.

questions.question: class A { static hello() { return "hi"; } } const a = new A(); What happens with a.hello()?
options: TypeError: a.hello is not a function
questions.correctAnswer: TypeError: a.hello is not a function
questions.answer:
Why B: Static methods live on the class itself, not on instances, so a.hello is undefined and calling it throws.

Why not A: That works with A.hello().

Why not C: Calling undefined throws, it does not return undefined.

Why not D: The code is valid syntax, the error happens at runtime.

questions.question: What happens if code outside the class tries to read obj.#count?
options: It throws a SyntaxError before the code runs
It throws a TypeError at runtime
questions.correctAnswer: It throws a SyntaxError before the code runs
questions.answer:
Why C: Private field names are checked when the code is parsed, and using #count outside its class is invalid syntax.

Why not A: The engine does not even run the line, so there is nothing to return.

Why not B: Private fields can never be read from outside the class.

Why not D: The error is a SyntaxError found when the code is parsed, not a TypeError while it runs.

questions.question: What does typeof class Example {} return?
questions.answer:
Why A: Classes are special functions underneath, so typeof gives "function".

Why not B: There is no "class" result from typeof.

Why not C: Instances are objects, but the class itself is a function.

Why not D: The class exists, so it is not undefined.

questions.question: class A {} class B extends A {} What does new B() instanceof A return?
options: false, because the object was created by B
true, because A.prototype is in the prototype chain of the object
true only if B has a constructor
questions.correctAnswer: true, because A.prototype is in the prototype chain of the object
questions.answer:
Why B: B.prototype inherits from A.prototype, so A.prototype is found in the object's chain.

Why not A: instanceof checks the whole chain, not just the direct class.

Why not C: instanceof works normally for subclasses.

Why not D: A constructor is not needed, the link exists through extends.

questions.question: What is the difference between map() and forEach()?
questions.answer:
Short answer: map() returns a new array with the result of the callback for every item. forEach() just runs the callback for each item and returns undefined. Use map when you need a new array, forEach for side effects like logging. How it works: map: same length as the original, transformed items, original unchanged forEach: returns undefined, cannot be chained Neither can break early: use for...of or some() for that React: map is used to turn data into JSX elements Example: Showing a list of course titles: courses.map((c) =>
  • {c.title}
    • ). forEach would return undefined and render nothing. Common mistake: Using map without using the result, only for side effects. It works, but it creates a throwaway array and tells readers the wrong intention. Interview tip: Say "map for transforming, forEach for doing". Then mention that neither waits for async callbacks, which leads into a common follow-up question.

questions.question: When do you use filter(), find(), findIndex(), some() and every()?
questions.answer:
Short answer: filter returns all matching items as an array. find returns the first match (or undefined). findIndex returns its position (or -1). some asks "is at least one true?" and every asks "are all true?".

How it works:
filter: [] if nothing matches, never undefined
find: first item or undefined, stops at the first match
findIndex: index or -1
some: true or false, stops at the first true
every: true or false, stops at the first false, and is true for an empty array
findLast / findLastIndex: search from the end

Example: In a quiz, answers.every((a) => a.selected !== null) checks that all questions are answered before submit, and answers.filter((a) => a.correct).length gives the score.

Common mistake: Using filter(...)[0] to get one item. find is clearer and stops early instead of scanning the whole array.

Interview tip: Mention that every on an empty array returns true. It surprises many people, and it can let an empty form pass a "all fields valid" check.

questions.question: How does reduce() work? Give practical examples.
questions.answer:
Short answer: reduce() walks through the array and builds one result step by step. The callback gets the accumulated value and the current item, and returns the new accumulated value. The second argument is the starting value.

How it works:
Signature: arr.reduce((acc, item) => newAcc, initialValue)
Sum: start at 0, add each item
Group: start with {}, push each item into its group
Count: start with {}, increase a counter per key
No initial value: the first item is used as the start, and an empty array throws

Example: A cart total: cart.reduce((sum, item) => sum + item.price * item.qty, 0). Counting answers per difficulty: questions.reduce((acc, q) => ({ ...acc, [q.difficulty]: (acc[q.difficulty] || 0) + 1 }), {}).

Common mistake: Leaving out the initial value. It works with numbers until the array is empty, then it throws "Reduce of empty array with no initial value".

Interview tip: Mention that readable code beats clever reduce. For simple grouping, Object.groupBy or a for...of loop is often clearer for teammates.

questions.question: Which array methods change the original array, and what are the non-mutating alternatives?
questions.answer:
Short answer: push, pop, shift, unshift, splice, sort, reverse, fill and copyWithin change the array in place. map, filter, slice, concat, spread and the newer toSorted, toReversed, toSpliced and with() return new arrays.

How it works:
Mutating: push, pop, shift, unshift, splice, sort, reverse, fill
Non-mutating: map, filter, slice, concat, [...arr]
New copies (ES2023): toSorted(), toReversed(), toSpliced(), with(index, value)
Why it matters: React state, Redux and shared data expect new arrays

Example: Showing a sorted leaderboard from props with players.sort(...) changes the parent's array during render. players.toSorted(...) or [...players].sort(...) keeps the original order intact.

Common mistake: Thinking sort() returns a sorted copy. It returns the same array, now sorted, so the original variable has changed too.

Interview tip: Mention the ES2023 copy methods by name. Knowing recent additions shows you keep your skills current, which remote employers value.

questions.question: What is the difference between slice() and splice()?
questions.answer:
Short answer: slice(start, end) copies a part of the array into a new array without changing the original. splice(start, deleteCount, ...items) changes the original array by removing and/or inserting items, and returns the removed items.

How it works:
slice: non-mutating, end index is not included, negative indexes count from the end
splice: mutating, returns an array of the removed items
slice(): with no arguments makes a shallow copy
toSpliced(): the non-mutating version of splice (ES2023)

Example: Pagination of an in-memory list: items.slice(20, 40) gives page 2 without touching items. Removing the third todo: todos.splice(2, 1) changes todos and returns [removedTodo].

Common mistake: Using splice in React state updates. It mutates the state array, so React may not re-render. Use filter or toSpliced instead.

Interview tip: Remember "slice is safe, splice is surgery". A short memory line like that helps you and the interviewer.
questions.codeSnippet:
const arr = [1, 2, 3, 4];
console.log(arr.slice(1, 3));     // [2, 3]
console.log(arr);                 // [1, 2, 3, 4]
console.log(arr.splice(1, 2));    // [2, 3]
console.log(arr);                 // [1, 4]

questions.question: When should you use a for loop, for...of, for...in or forEach?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Use for...of for most array loops, a classic for loop when you need the index or best speed, forEach for short side-effect callbacks, and for...in only for object keys (never for arrays).

How it works:
for (let i = 0; ...): index control, can break, fastest in hot code
for...of: values of any iterable (arrays, strings, Map, Set), can break and await
forEach: clean callback style, cannot break, does not wait for async
for...in: enumerable keys including inherited ones, keys are strings

Example: Sending 50 emails one by one with a delay needs for (const user of users) { await send(user); }. forEach would start all 50 at once and not wait.

Common mistake: Using for...in on an array. Indexes come back as strings ("0", "1"), and any extra enumerable property on the array or its prototype is included too.

Interview tip: Mention entries() for when you need both index and value in for...of: for (const [i, user] of users.entries()).

questions.question: Why does [10, 1, 2].sort() return [1, 10, 2], and how do you sort correctly?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Without a compare function, sort() converts items to strings and sorts them in dictionary order, so "10" comes before "2". Pass a compare function: (a, b) => a - b for numbers, localeCompare for text.

How it works:
Default: string order by UTF-16 code units
Numbers: (a, b) => a - b ascending, (a, b) => b - a descending
Strings: a.localeCompare(b) for correct language order
Objects: (a, b) => a.score - b.score, or compare several keys
Stable: since ES2019, equal items keep their original order

Example: A leaderboard sorted with scores.sort() shows 100 between 1 and 20. With (a, b) => b - a, the highest score is first.

Common mistake: Returning a boolean from the compare function, like (a, b) => a > b. It must return a negative, zero or positive number, so a boolean gives wrong results in some engines.

Interview tip: Mention sorting by two keys, like by score then by name: (a, b) => b.score - a.score || a.name.localeCompare(b.name). It shows you can handle real requirements.

questions.question: How do you remove duplicates from an array and group items by a key in modern JavaScript?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Remove duplicate primitives with [...new Set(arr)]. For objects, keep a Set or Map of seen keys. Group items with Object.groupBy(arr, fn) (ES2024) or Map.groupBy, or with reduce in older environments.

How it works:
Primitives: [...new Set([1, 1, 2])] gives [1, 2]
Objects by key: new Map(arr.map((x) => [x.id, x])).values() keeps the last of each id
Object.groupBy: returns a null-prototype object of arrays, keys become strings
Map.groupBy: keys can be any value, like objects or numbers
Order: Set and Map keep insertion order

Example: Questions grouped by topic for a sidebar: Object.groupBy(questions, (q) => q.topic) gives { "Closures": [...], "Promises": [...] } in one line.

Common mistake: Using new Set on an array of objects and expecting duplicates to disappear. Objects are compared by reference, so two equal-looking objects both stay.

Interview tip: Mention checking support (Object.groupBy needs Node 21+ and recent browsers) and showing the reduce fallback. It shows care about where code runs.

questions.question: Why does async/await inside forEach not wait, and how do you run async work on an array correctly?
questions.answer:
Short answer: forEach ignores the Promises returned by an async callback, so the loop finishes immediately and the code after it runs before the work is done. Use for...of with await for one-by-one, or Promise.all with map for parallel work.

How it works:
forEach: calls the callback, throws away its returned Promise
for...of + await: sequential, one finishes before the next starts
Promise.all(arr.map(async ...)): parallel, waits for all
Limited parallel: process in batches (or use a helper like p-limit) to avoid overloading an API

Example: An admin bulk-import does items.forEach(async (q) => await Question.create(q)); then res.json({ done: true }). The response says done while the inserts are still running, and errors are never caught.

Common mistake: Fixing it with await items.forEach(...). forEach returns undefined, so the await does nothing.

Interview tip: Explain when to choose sequential (order matters, rate limits) vs parallel (independent and fast). That judgement is what interviewers look for.

questions.question: What are array-like objects, and how do Array.from() and the spread operator convert them?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Array-like objects have numbered indexes and a length but no array methods, like arguments, a NodeList or { length: 2, 0: 'a', 1: 'b' }. Array.from() turns array-likes and iterables into real arrays, while spread [...x] only works on iterables.

How it works:
Array.from(arrayLike): works with length plus indexes
Array.from(iterable): works with Set, Map, strings, NodeList
Mapping: Array.from({ length: 5 }, (_, i) => i) builds [0, 1, 2, 3, 4]
Spread: requires Symbol.iterator, so a plain { length: 2 } object fails
NodeList: has forEach, but not map or filter

Example: Turning all checked boxes into ids: Array.from(document.querySelectorAll('input:checked'), (el) => el.value). One call converts and maps.

Common mistake: Using new Array(5).map(...) to build a range. new Array(5) has empty slots, and map skips empty slots, so you still get 5 empty items.

Interview tip: Mention Array.from({ length: n }, fn) as the clean way to create ranges and test data. It is a small trick that looks professional.

questions.question: What is the difference between an array and a linked list? How would you build a simple linked list in JavaScript?
questions.answer:
Short answer: An array keeps items in order with fast index access (O(1)), but inserting or removing at the start or middle shifts items (O(n)). A linked list stores nodes that point to the next node: inserting or removing at a known node is O(1), but reaching the i-th item is O(n).

How it works:
Access by index: array O(1), linked list O(n)
Insert or delete at the start: array O(n) (unshift and shift move everything), linked list O(1)
Memory: array items sit together (fast for the CPU cache); list nodes are scattered and each one stores an extra pointer
JavaScript arrays grow automatically; there is no built-in linked list, so you write a Node class

Example: A playlist where songs are often inserted in the middle fits a linked list. A product list that you index, sort and filter fits an array.

Common mistake: Saying a linked list is always faster for inserts. You first have to walk to the right node, which is O(n).

Interview tip: Draw boxes and arrows while you explain. Follow-ups are usually stacks, queues or reversing the list.

questions.question: How do you implement a stack and a queue in JavaScript, and why can array.shift() be slow for a large queue?
questions.answer:
Short answer: A stack is last in, first out: push() and pop() at the end of an array, both O(1). A queue is first in, first out: add at the end and remove from the front. shift() moves every remaining item one place, so it is O(n); for big queues keep a head index or use a linked list.

How it works:
Stack: push() adds, pop() removes the last item
Queue with shift(): simple, but O(n) per removal
Queue with a head index: dequeue only moves the index, O(1)
Clean up: reset or slice the array now and then so memory does not grow forever

Example: The browser back button works like a stack. A job list of emails to send works like a queue.

Common mistake: Calling shift() inside a loop over 100,000 jobs. That turns the whole loop into O(n^2).

Interview tip: Mention a real use: a stack for undo or matching brackets, a queue for breadth-first search or background jobs.

questions.question: Which method returns a new array with every item transformed by a callback?
questions.answer:
Why C: map() calls the callback for each item and returns a new array of the results.

Why not A: forEach() returns undefined.

Why not B: filter() keeps or removes items, it does not transform them.

Why not D: find() returns a single item, not a new array.

questions.question: What is stored in r after const r = [1, 2, 3].forEach((n) => n * 2);?
questions.answer:
Why B: forEach always returns undefined, whatever the callback returns.

Why not A: That would be the result of map().

Why not C: forEach does not return the original array either.

Why not D: forEach does not add up the values.

questions.question: What does [1, 2, 3, 4].filter((n) => n % 2) return?
questions.answer:
Why A: n % 2 is 1 (truthy) for odd numbers and 0 (falsy) for even ones, so filter keeps 1 and 3.

Why not B: Even numbers give 0, which is falsy, so they are removed.

Why not C: filter keeps the original items, not the callback results.

Why not D: That would be map, which returns the callback results.

questions.question: const arr = [1, 2, 3]; const removed = arr.splice(1, 1); What are removed and arr?
questions.answer:
Why D: splice(1, 1) removes one item at index 1 and returns the removed items as an array.

Why not A: splice always returns an array, even for one item.

Why not B: Index 1 is the second item, the value 2.

Why not C: The second argument says to remove only one item.

questions.question: What does [10, 1, 2].sort() return?
questions.answer:
Why C: Without a compare function, items are compared as strings, and "10" comes before "2" in dictionary order.

Why not A: That needs a numeric compare function, (a, b) => a - b.

Why not B: That is descending numeric order.

Why not D: No ordering rule produces this result.

questions.question: What happens with [].reduce((a, b) => a + b)?
options: Throws a TypeError: Reduce of empty array with no initial value
questions.correctAnswer: Throws a TypeError: Reduce of empty array with no initial value
questions.answer:
Why D: Without an initial value, reduce uses the first item as the start, and an empty array has none, so it throws.

Why not A: You get 0 only if you pass 0 as the initial value.

Why not B: reduce throws instead of returning undefined.

Why not C: No addition happens, so NaN cannot appear.

Fix: [].reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0)

questions.question: How does destructuring work for objects and arrays, including default values and renaming?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Destructuring pulls values out of objects or arrays into variables in one line. Objects match by property name, arrays match by position. You can rename, set defaults and collect the rest.

How it works:
Object: const { name, age } = user
Rename: const { name: userName } = user
Default: const { role = 'user' } = user, used only when the value is undefined
Array: const [first, second] = list, skip with commas: const [, second] = list
Nested: const { address: { city } } = user
Function parameters: function show({ title, price = 0 }) { ... }

Example: React props and hooks use it everywhere: const [count, setCount] = useState(0) and function Card({ title, onClick }).

Common mistake: Destructuring a nested object that might be missing, like const { address: { city } } = user when address is undefined. It throws "Cannot read properties of undefined". Add a default: { address: { city } = {} }.

Interview tip: Show a function with destructured options and defaults. It is the most practical use and makes calls self-documenting.

questions.question: What is the difference between the spread operator and rest parameters?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Both use ..., but they do opposite jobs. Spread expands an array or object into separate items. Rest collects several items into one array or object.

How it works:
Spread in arrays: [...a, ...b] joins arrays
Spread in objects: { ...defaults, ...options } merges, later keys win
Spread in calls: Math.max(...nums)
Rest in parameters: function log(level, ...messages)
Rest in destructuring: const { password, ...safeUser } = user

Example: Before sending a user to the frontend, const { password, ...safeUser } = user removes the password in one line, and res.json(safeUser) sends the rest.

Common mistake: Expecting spread to copy deeply. { ...user } copies only the top level, nested objects are still shared.

Interview tip: Say "spread unpacks, rest packs". Then show the password-removal example, which is short and very practical.

questions.question: What are template literals, and what are tagged templates used for?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Template literals use backticks and allow ${expressions} and multi-line strings. A tagged template runs a function on the string parts and values, which libraries use for safe SQL, styled CSS and translations. How it works: Interpolation: `Hello ${name}` calls String on the value Multi-line: line breaks are kept as written Tag: tag`text ${value}` calls tag(strings, ...values) String.raw: a built-in tag that keeps backslashes as written Uses: styled-components css, GraphQL gql, SQL builders that escape values Example: A SQL helper sql`SELECT * FROM users WHERE id = ${id}` receives id separately and sends it as a parameter, so user input cannot break the query. Common mistake: Building HTML with template literals and user input, like el.innerHTML = `

${comment}

`. That allows XSS if the comment contains HTML. Interview tip: Mention styled-components or gql as tagged templates you have seen. It shows you recognise the feature in real libraries.

questions.question: How do optional chaining (?.) and nullish coalescing (??) work, and how is ?? different from ||?
questions.answer:
Short answer: ?. stops and returns undefined if the value before it is null or undefined, instead of throwing. ?? gives a fallback only when the left side is null or undefined, while || also replaces 0, "" and false.

How it works:
user?.address?.city: undefined if user or address is missing
obj.method?.(): calls only if the method exists
arr?.[0]: safe index access
a ?? b: b only when a is null or undefined
a || b: b when a is any falsy value
??=: assign only if the variable is null or undefined

Example: Showing a quiz score: score ?? 'Not attempted'. With ||, a real score of 0 would wrongly show "Not attempted".

Common mistake: Overusing ?. everywhere. It hides real bugs, because a required value that is missing silently becomes undefined instead of failing early.

Interview tip: Say you use ?. for data that is truly optional (API fields that may be missing), and let required data fail loudly. That balance impresses reviewers.

questions.question: When should you use Map and Set instead of plain objects and arrays, and what are WeakMap and WeakSet?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Use Map when keys are not strings, when you add and remove keys often, or when you need the size and insertion order easily. Use Set for unique values and fast "has" checks. WeakMap and WeakSet hold object keys weakly, so they do not stop garbage collection.

How it works:
Map: any key type, map.size, keeps insertion order, easy to iterate
Object: string or symbol keys, inherited keys can collide (like "constructor")
Set: unique values, set.has(x) is fast compared with array.includes on big lists
WeakMap: keys must be objects, entries disappear when the key object is gone
Weak types: cannot be iterated and have no size

Example: Tracking online users: const online = new Set(); online.add(userId) and online.has(userId) are fast and never give duplicates.

Common mistake: Sending a Map in an API response with res.json(map). JSON.stringify turns it into {}, so convert with Object.fromEntries(map) first.

Interview tip: Mention WeakMap for caching data about DOM nodes or objects without causing memory leaks. It shows you think about memory, not only syntax.

questions.question: How do ES module imports and exports work, and what is the difference between named and default exports?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Each file is a module with its own scope. export makes values available, import brings them in. A file can have many named exports but only one default export.

How it works:
Named export: export const add = ...; import { add } from './math.js'
Rename: import { add as sum } from './math.js'
Default export: export default App; import App from './App.jsx' (any name)
Namespace: import * as math from './math.js'
Live bindings: imports see the exporter's current value, and are read-only
Static: imports are hoisted and resolved before the code runs

Example: A React project exports components as default (one per file) and helpers as named exports (many per utils file), which keeps imports predictable.

Common mistake: Mixing them up, like import { App } from './App' when App is a default export. The value is undefined and React shows "Element type is invalid".

Interview tip: Mention that many teams prefer named exports because editors can auto-import and rename them safely, and typos fail at build time.

questions.question: What are iterators and generators, and where are they useful in real code?
questions.answer:
Short answer: An iterator is an object with a next() method that returns { value, done }. A generator function (function*) creates an iterator easily: each yield pauses the function and hands out a value. They produce values lazily, one at a time.

How it works:
Iterable: has [Symbol.iterator](), usable in for...of and spread
Generator: function* with yield, call it to get an iterator
Lazy: values are created only when requested
Infinite sequences: possible, because nothing is computed ahead
Async generators: async function* with for await...of, for paged APIs

Example: Fetching all pages from a paginated API with an async generator: for await (const page of fetchPages('/api/questions')) handles 10 or 10,000 pages with the same code and low memory.

Common mistake: Spreading an infinite generator, like [...ids()]. It never finishes and freezes the program.

Interview tip: Mention that Redux-Saga is built on generators and that async generators are great for streaming. Real references make the answer stronger.

questions.question: Which newer JavaScript features (ES2022 to ES2024) are worth knowing for interviews?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Useful recent additions include at(), Object.hasOwn(), structuredClone(), top-level await, class private fields, Array findLast, the copy methods (toSorted, toReversed, toSpliced, with) and Object.groupBy.

How it works:
at(-1): last item without arr[arr.length - 1]
Object.hasOwn(obj, key): safer than obj.hasOwnProperty(key)
structuredClone(): built-in deep copy
Top-level await: await in ES modules without an async wrapper
#private fields and static blocks in classes
findLast / findLastIndex: search from the end
toSorted, toReversed, toSpliced, with: copies instead of mutation
Object.groupBy / Map.groupBy: group items in one call

Example: Getting the latest message in a chat: messages.at(-1). Updating one item in React state immutably: setItems(items.with(index, newItem)).

Common mistake: Using new features without checking where the code runs. Older browsers or Node versions may need a polyfill or a newer runtime.

Interview tip: Mention one or two you actually use. Remote interviewers like candidates who keep up with the language but stay practical about support.
questions.codeSnippet:
const msgs = ['hi', 'hello', 'bye'];
console.log(msgs.at(-1));                       // "bye"
console.log(msgs.with(0, 'hey'));               // ['hey', 'hello', 'bye']
console.log(Object.hasOwn({ a: 1 }, 'a'));      // true
console.log([1, 5, 8, 3].findLast((n) => n > 4)); // 8

questions.question: What are Proxy and Reflect, and what are they used for in practice?
questions.answer:
Short answer: A Proxy wraps an object and lets you intercept operations on it, like reading, writing or deleting properties, through handler functions called traps. Reflect provides the default behaviour for those operations, so traps can forward to it.

How it works:
get trap: runs on obj.prop
set trap: runs on obj.prop = value, can validate
has, deleteProperty, apply and more: other operations
Reflect.get / Reflect.set: do the normal operation inside a trap
Uses: validation, logging, default values, reactivity (Vue 3), API clients

Example: A settings object wrapped in a Proxy rejects unknown keys and wrong types, so a typo like settings.thme = 'dark' throws right away instead of silently creating a new property.

Common mistake: Using Proxies in hot code paths. Every property access goes through a function, which is slower than normal objects.

Interview tip: Mention that Vue 3's reactivity system is built on Proxy. Linking an advanced feature to a well-known framework makes the answer memorable.

questions.question: What are dynamic import() and top-level await, and how do they help performance?
questions.answer:
Short answer: import() loads a module at runtime and returns a Promise, so code can be split and loaded only when needed. Top-level await lets an ES module use await outside any function, for example to load config before exporting.

How it works:
import('./heavy.js'): returns a Promise of the module
Code splitting: bundlers like Vite create a separate file for each dynamic import
React: lazy(() => import('./AdminPage')) loads the page on first visit
Top-level await: works only in ES modules, and pauses modules that import this one
Errors: a failed dynamic import rejects, so handle it

Example: A big chart library is only used on the admin dashboard. Loading it with import() keeps it out of the main bundle, so the public pages load much faster on mobile.

Common mistake: Using top-level await for slow network calls in a shared module. Every module that imports it waits, which can delay the whole app's start.

Interview tip: Mention measuring the bundle (for example with a bundle visualiser) before and after splitting. Numbers make performance answers convincing.

questions.question: const { a, ...rest } = { a: 1, b: 2, c: 3 }; What is rest?
questions.answer:
Why A: The rest pattern collects all remaining own properties into a new object.

Why not B: Object rest creates an object, not an array.

Why not C: a was already taken out, so it is not in rest.

Why not D: rest always gets an object, even if it is empty.

questions.question: What does 0 ?? "default" return?
questions.answer:
Why C: ?? only uses the right side when the left side is null or undefined, and 0 is neither.

Why not A: That is the result of 0 || "default", because || replaces any falsy value.

Why not B: The expression returns one of its two sides.

Why not D: null is not involved in this expression.

questions.question: With const user = undefined;, what does user?.address?.city return?
questions.answer:
Why B: Optional chaining stops at the first null or undefined and returns undefined.

Why not A: That would happen with user.address.city without ?.

Why not C: Optional chaining returns undefined, never null.

Why not D: No string is created.

questions.question: What is new Set([1, 1, 2, 2, 3]).size?
questions.answer:
Why D: A Set keeps only unique values, so it stores 1, 2 and 3.

Why not A: Duplicates are not stored, so it is not 5.

Why not B: There are three different values, not two.

Why not C: Only exact duplicates are removed, so more than one value remains.

questions.question: const [a = 1] = [null]; What is a?
questions.answer:
Why B: Default values in destructuring apply only when the value is undefined. null is a real value, so a becomes null.

Why not A: That would happen with [] or [undefined].

Why not C: The array has a value at index 0, and it is null.

Why not D: Destructuring null inside an array is fine. Only destructuring null itself throws.

questions.question: function* g() { yield 1; yield 2; } const it = g(); it.next(); it.next(); What does a third it.next() return?
questions.answer:
Why D: After the last yield, the generator finishes, so next() returns done: true with value undefined (there is no return value).

Why not A: The second call already returned { value: 2, done: false }.

Why not B: Generators do not restart from the beginning.

Why not C: Calling next() on a finished generator is allowed and keeps returning done: true.

questions.question: What is asynchronous code, and why does JavaScript need it?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Asynchronous code starts a slow task (a network request, a timer, reading a file) and continues with other work instead of waiting. JavaScript runs on one main thread, so without async code one slow request would freeze the whole page or server.

How it works:
Synchronous: each line waits for the previous one to finish
Asynchronous: the slow task runs in the background (browser or Node), and a callback or Promise handles the result later
Tools: callbacks, Promises, async/await
Event loop: picks up finished tasks when the main thread is free

Example: While a page fetches the question list from the API, the user can still scroll, type and click. When the data arrives, React updates the list.

Common mistake: Expecting an async value on the next line, like const data = fetch(url); console.log(data.items). data is a Promise, not the response.

Interview tip: Use the restaurant analogy: a waiter takes your order to the kitchen and serves other tables instead of standing at the stove. Then name the three tools in order of history.

questions.question: What is callback hell, and how do Promises and async/await solve it?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Callback hell is deeply nested callbacks, where each async step is placed inside the previous one's callback. The code drifts to the right, errors must be handled at every level, and it becomes hard to read. Promises flatten it into a chain, and async/await makes it look like normal top-to-bottom code.

How it works:
Callbacks: nested functions, error handled separately at each step
Promises: .then() chains, one .catch() at the end
async/await: sequential-looking code with try/catch
Same work: all three do the same async steps underneath

Example: Login, then load profile, then load courses, then load progress. With callbacks this is four levels deep. With async/await it is four lines, one under the other.

Common mistake: Nesting .then() calls inside each other, recreating callback hell with Promises. Return the next Promise from .then() so the chain stays flat.

Interview tip: Show the same three-step flow in both styles. A visual before and after is the most convincing answer.

questions.question: What is a Promise, and what states can it be in?
questions.answer:
Short answer: A Promise is an object that represents a value that will be ready later. It starts as pending, and then settles once: either fulfilled with a value or rejected with an error. After settling it never changes.

How it works:
pending: still working
fulfilled: success, .then() handlers get the value
rejected: failure, .catch() handlers get the reason
Settled once: calling resolve or reject again does nothing
Creating: new Promise((resolve, reject) => ...), usually only to wrap old callback APIs

Example: fetch('/api/courses') returns a Promise right away. When the response arrives it is fulfilled, and if the network is down it is rejected.

Common mistake: Creating new Promise around code that already returns a Promise, like new Promise((res) => fetch(url).then(res)). Errors get lost, because the reject path is never connected.

Interview tip: Mention that .then always returns a new Promise, which is what makes chaining possible. It shows you understand how Promises compose.

questions.question: How do you handle errors with async/await, and what happens to an error you do not catch?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Wrap awaits in try/catch, or call .catch() on the Promise returned by the async function. An error you do not catch rejects the Promise, and if nobody handles it, it becomes an unhandled rejection (a console error in browsers, a crash in modern Node).

How it works:
try/catch: catches both thrown errors and rejected awaits
finally: runs either way, good for hiding a loading spinner
async function: always returns a Promise, a throw inside rejects it
Callers: must await or .catch() it, or the error escapes

Example: A React submit handler does setLoading(true), then try { await api.save(form) } catch (e) { setError(e.message) } finally { setLoading(false) }. The spinner always stops, even when saving fails.

Common mistake: Calling an async function without await or .catch(), like saveDraft();. If it fails, nothing handles the error, and in Node the process can exit.

Interview tip: Mention that try/catch only catches what you await. return promise inside try is not caught there, but return await promise is.

questions.question: What is the difference between Promise.all, Promise.allSettled, Promise.race and Promise.any?
questions.answer:
Short answer: All four take a list of Promises. all waits for every one and fails fast on the first error. allSettled waits for every one and reports each result. race settles with the first one to settle. any resolves with the first success and fails only if all fail.

How it works:
all: array of values, rejects on the first rejection
allSettled: [{ status, value or reason }], never rejects
race: first settled, success or failure
any: first fulfilled, rejects with AggregateError if all reject

Example: A dashboard loads stats, users and courses together. With allSettled, if the courses API fails, the stats and users still show, and only the courses card shows an error.

Common mistake: Using Promise.all for independent widgets. One failing request makes the whole page show an error even though the other data loaded fine.

Interview tip: Mention a race use case: Promise.race([fetch(url), timeout(5000)]) to give up on a slow request. A practical example for each method sounds experienced.

questions.question: Why can several awaits in a row make your code slow, and how do you run independent requests in parallel?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Each await waits for the previous one to finish. If the requests do not depend on each other, start them all first and then await them together with Promise.all, so the total time is the slowest one instead of the sum.

How it works:
Sequential: await a(); await b(); await c(); takes a + b + c
Parallel: await Promise.all([a(), b(), c()]) takes about the max
Dependent steps: must stay sequential (you need the user id before loading their orders)
Too much parallel: thousands at once can overload an API, so batch them

Example: A profile page awaits user (300 ms), then badges (300 ms), then stats (300 ms): 900 ms. Using Promise.all for the three independent calls loads in about 300 ms.

Common mistake: Writing const a = await getA(); const b = await getB(); out of habit, even when getB does not need a.

Interview tip: Show the timing numbers. Saying "900 ms became 300 ms" makes the answer concrete and shows you think about user experience.

questions.question: Why does fetch() not throw on a 404 or 500 response, and how should you handle errors with fetch?
questions.answer:
Short answer: fetch only rejects when the request could not be made at all (network down, DNS failure, CORS block). A 404 or 500 is still a successful HTTP exchange, so the Promise resolves. You must check response.ok (or response.status) yourself.

How it works:
Rejects: network errors, aborts, CORS failures
Resolves: every HTTP status, including 400 and 500
response.ok: true for status 200 to 299
Body: read the error JSON with await response.json() before throwing
Wrapper: one small helper that throws on !ok keeps every call clean

Example: The login page calls fetch('/api/login'). Wrong password returns 401, the code skips the error and tries to read data.token, so the user sees nothing happen. Checking res.ok shows "Invalid email or password".

Common mistake: Putting only a .catch() on fetch and assuming it handles server errors. It does not run for 4xx or 5xx responses.

Interview tip: Mention that axios behaves differently (it rejects for non-2xx statuses). Knowing the difference shows you have used both.

questions.question: How do you cancel a fetch request or add a timeout with AbortController?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Create an AbortController, pass controller.signal to fetch, and call controller.abort() to cancel. For a timeout, use AbortSignal.timeout(ms). An aborted fetch rejects with an AbortError (or TimeoutError for the timeout signal).

How it works:
Controller: const c = new AbortController(); fetch(url, { signal: c.signal })
Cancel: c.abort() stops the request and rejects the Promise
Timeout: fetch(url, { signal: AbortSignal.timeout(5000) })
React: abort in the useEffect cleanup when the component unmounts or inputs change
Ignore aborts: check err.name === 'AbortError' so you do not show an error toast

Example: A search page fetches results on each keystroke. Aborting the previous request when the user types again saves bandwidth and prevents old results from appearing.

Common mistake: Not handling the AbortError, so every normal cancel shows a red "Request failed" message to the user.

Interview tip: Mention that Node's fetch and many Node APIs (like timers and streams) also accept an AbortSignal. It is one pattern you can use everywhere.

questions.question: How do you retry a failing request with exponential backoff?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Retry a few times, and wait longer after each failure (for example 500 ms, 1 s, 2 s), plus a little random "jitter". Only retry errors that can fix themselves, like network failures, 429 and 503, never 400 or 401.

How it works:
Attempts: a small maximum, like 3 to 5
Delay: base * 2 ** attempt, plus random jitter
Retry only: network errors, timeouts, 429, 502, 503, 504
Do not retry: validation errors, auth errors, 404
Respect Retry-After: servers may tell you how long to wait

Example: A free-tier API wakes up slowly after sleeping. The first request times out, the retry 1 second later succeeds, and the user never sees an error.

Common mistake: Retrying immediately in a tight loop. When a server is struggling, thousands of clients doing that make the outage worse (a "retry storm").

Interview tip: Mention idempotency: only retry requests that are safe to repeat, or use an idempotency key, so a retried payment is not charged twice.

questions.question: A search box shows wrong results: the user types "react", but results for "rea" appear last. What causes this race condition, and how do you fix it?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Each keystroke starts a request, and responses can arrive out of order. If the request for "rea" is slower than the one for "react", it finishes last and overwrites the correct results. Fix it by ignoring or cancelling outdated requests.

How it works: Ways to fix it:
Abort: cancel the previous request with AbortController before starting a new one
Ignore: keep a request id or flag, and only apply the latest response
Debounce: wait until typing pauses (for example 300 ms) to send fewer requests
Libraries: React Query or SWR handle this for you

Example: Typing "react" sends 5 requests. Without a fix, the final screen depends on network luck. With an "ignore stale" flag in the useEffect cleanup, only the "react" results are ever shown.

Common mistake: Adding only debounce. It reduces requests, but two requests can still overlap and arrive out of order.

Interview tip: Name the problem ("race condition from out-of-order responses") and give two fixes. This is a classic front-end interview question, and a clear answer stands out.

questions.question: What are the three states of a Promise?
questions.answer:
Why B: A Promise starts pending and then becomes fulfilled (success) or rejected (failure).

Why not A: These are not the official Promise states.

Why not C: These describe the idea, but the official names are fulfilled and rejected.

Why not D: open and closed are not Promise states.

questions.question: Promise.all receives three Promises and the second one rejects. What happens?
options: Promise.all waits and returns the two successful values
Promise.all resolves with undefined for the failed one
Promise.all rejects with the first rejection reason, without waiting for the rest
The other two Promises are cancelled automatically
questions.correctAnswer: Promise.all rejects with the first rejection reason, without waiting for the rest
questions.answer:
Why C: Promise.all fails fast: the first rejection rejects the combined Promise.

Why not A: Waiting and reporting each result is what Promise.allSettled does.

Why not B: Promise.all never fills in undefined for failures.

Why not D: Promises cannot be cancelled. The other requests keep running, their results are just ignored.

questions.question: What does an async function always return?
options: The value in its return statement
questions.answer:
Why D: An async function always returns a Promise, which resolves with the returned value or rejects with a thrown error.

Why not A: The returned value is wrapped in a Promise, so you need await or .then() to get it.

Why not B: Even with no return statement, you get a Promise that resolves to undefined.

Why not C: async functions do not return callbacks.

questions.question: fetch("/api/missing") gets a 404 response. What happens?
options: The Promise resolves, and response.ok is false
The Promise rejects with a 404 error
questions.correctAnswer: The Promise resolves, and response.ok is false
questions.answer:
Why A: fetch resolves for any HTTP response, and ok is true only for statuses 200 to 299.

Why not B: fetch rejects only for network-level failures, not HTTP error statuses.

Why not C: fetch never retries on its own.

Why not D: The server replied, so the Promise settles.

questions.question: What happens when every Promise passed to Promise.any() rejects?
options: It rejects with the first error
It rejects with an AggregateError containing all the errors
It resolves with an array of the errors
questions.correctAnswer: It rejects with an AggregateError containing all the errors
questions.answer:
Why C: Promise.any only fails when there is no success at all, and then it rejects with an AggregateError listing every reason.

Why not A: A total failure is never turned into a success.

Why not B: Rejecting with the first error is how Promise.all behaves.

Why not D: An array of outcomes is what Promise.allSettled gives.

questions.question: const r = await Promise.allSettled([Promise.resolve(1), Promise.reject("x")]); What is r[1]?
questions.answer:
Why B: allSettled reports each Promise as an object with a status, and rejected ones carry their reason.

Why not A: allSettled wraps every result in a status object.

Why not C: The second Promise was rejected, not fulfilled.

Why not D: allSettled never rejects, so the await does not throw.

questions.question: What is the event loop in JavaScript? Explain it in simple words.
questions.answer:
Short answer: JavaScript runs your code on one thread, one piece at a time. The event loop is the system that waits until the current code finishes, then takes the next ready task (a finished timer, a click, a network response) and runs it.

How it works:
Call stack: the code running right now
Background work: timers, network and file reads are handled by the browser or Node, not by your thread
Queues: finished background work waits in queues
Event loop: when the stack is empty, it moves the next task onto the stack
One at a time: a task always runs to the end before the next one starts

Example: You click a button while a long loop is running. The click handler does not run in the middle of the loop. It waits in the queue and runs only after the loop finishes, which is why the page feels frozen.

Common mistake: Thinking async code runs "in parallel" with your JavaScript. Only the waiting happens in the background. Your callbacks still run one by one on the same thread.

Interview tip: Use the analogy of a single cashier with a queue of customers: fast, as long as no customer takes forever. Then mention microtasks, which is usually the next question.

questions.question: How do the call stack, Web APIs (or Node APIs), the task queue and the microtask queue work together?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Code runs on the call stack. Async operations are handed to the browser or Node. When they finish, their callbacks are queued: Promise callbacks go to the microtask queue, timers and events go to the task (macrotask) queue. After each task, the event loop empties the microtask queue before taking the next task.

How it works:
Call stack: functions being executed right now
Web APIs / Node APIs: setTimeout, fetch, DOM events, file system
Microtask queue: Promise .then, await continuations, queueMicrotask
Task queue: setTimeout, setInterval, I/O callbacks, UI events
Order: run one task, then all microtasks, then (in browsers) maybe render, then the next task

Example: A fetch finishes and its .then runs as a microtask right after the current code, before an older setTimeout(fn, 0) that is still waiting in the task queue.

Common mistake: Thinking timers run exactly on time. A setTimeout of 100 ms means "not before 100 ms", and it can be much later if the stack is busy.

Interview tip: Draw four boxes (stack, APIs, microtasks, tasks) with arrows. A drawing is the clearest way to explain this live.

questions.question: What is the difference between microtasks and macrotasks, and which run first?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Microtasks (Promise callbacks, await continuations, queueMicrotask) run right after the current script or task finishes, and all of them run before the next macrotask. Macrotasks (setTimeout, setInterval, events, I/O) run one per loop turn.

How it works:
Microtasks: Promise.then, catch, finally, code after await, queueMicrotask, MutationObserver
Macrotasks: setTimeout, setInterval, setImmediate (Node), DOM events, network callbacks
Rule: after each macrotask, drain the whole microtask queue
New microtasks: added during draining also run before the next macrotask

Example: Promise.resolve().then(a) and setTimeout(b, 0) scheduled together always run a first, then b, no matter which line came first.

Common mistake: Saying "setTimeout 0 runs immediately". It always waits for the current code and all pending microtasks.

Interview tip: Give a short rule: "sync code, then all microtasks, then one macrotask, repeat". It solves most output puzzles in seconds.

questions.question: Why does setTimeout(fn, 0) not run immediately?
questions.answer:
Short answer: setTimeout only puts fn in the task queue after the delay. It can run only when the call stack is empty and all microtasks are done, so it always waits for the current code to finish. Browsers may also add a minimum delay of about 4 ms for nested timers.

How it works:
Delay 0: means "as soon as possible", not "now"
Waits for: the rest of the current script, then all microtasks
Nested timers: after several nested levels, browsers clamp the delay to at least 4 ms
Busy thread: a long loop delays every timer

Example: A developer uses setTimeout(() => input.focus(), 0) to focus an input after React renders it. It works because the timer runs after the current rendering code finishes.

Common mistake: Using setTimeout(fn, 0) to "fix" ordering bugs without understanding them. It hides the real timing problem and breaks again on slower devices.

Interview tip: Mention better tools for specific jobs: queueMicrotask for "right after this code", requestAnimationFrame for "before the next paint", and useEffect for "after React renders".

questions.question: How does async/await relate to the microtask queue?
questions.answer:
Short answer: await pauses the async function and returns control to the caller. The rest of the function (the code after await) is scheduled as a microtask once the awaited Promise settles. So code after await always runs later, even if the value is already available.

How it works:
Before await: runs synchronously, like normal code
At await: the function pauses, the caller continues
After await: resumes as a microtask
await on a non-Promise: still pauses, and resumes as a microtask
Return value: the async function's Promise resolves when it finishes

Example: async function f() { console.log(1); await null; console.log(2); } f(); console.log(3); prints 1, 3, 2. The line after await waits for the current script to end.

Common mistake: Thinking an async function runs fully in the background. Everything before the first await runs immediately, and a heavy loop there still blocks the caller.

Interview tip: Explain await as "the rest of this function becomes a .then callback". That mental model makes every output question easy.

questions.question: How is the event loop in Node.js different from the browser event loop?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Both run callbacks one at a time and drain microtasks between tasks. Node's loop is organised in phases (timers, I/O callbacks, poll, check, close) and adds process.nextTick, which runs even before Promise microtasks. Browsers add rendering steps and requestAnimationFrame.

How it works:
Node phases: timers, pending callbacks, poll (I/O), check (setImmediate), close
process.nextTick: Node only, runs before Promise microtasks
setImmediate: Node only, runs in the check phase after I/O
Browser extras: rendering, requestAnimationFrame, user input events
Shared: Promises are microtasks in both

Example: Inside an I/O callback in Node, setImmediate always runs before setTimeout(fn, 0). In the main script their order can vary, which surprises people.

Common mistake: Using process.nextTick heavily for scheduling. Too many nextTick calls can starve I/O, because the loop cannot move to the next phase until they finish.

Interview tip: Mention that the same rule still applies in both: one thing at a time, and CPU-heavy code blocks everything. That is the practical takeaway.

questions.question: Predict the output and explain each step: a mix of console.log, setTimeout, Promise.then and an async function.
questions.answer:
Short answer: The output is: start, async start, end, promise, async end, timeout. Synchronous code runs first, then microtasks in the order they were queued, then the timer.

How it works: Step by step:
Step 1: "start" is logged (sync)
Step 2: setTimeout schedules a macrotask
Step 3: Promise.then queues microtask 1
Step 4: run() logs "async start", then await queues the rest as microtask 2
Step 5: "end" is logged (sync)
Step 6: microtask 1 logs "promise", microtask 2 logs "async end"
Step 7: the macrotask logs "timeout"

Example: These puzzles mirror real bugs, like a loading flag set in a .then running before or after a timer that hides a spinner.

Common mistake: Thinking "async end" runs right after "async start" because nothing slow is awaited. Any await, even of a resolved value, defers the rest to a microtask.

Interview tip: Talk through the queues out loud while writing the answer. Interviewers care more about the process than the final list.

questions.question: A heavy calculation freezes the page for 3 seconds. Why, and how can you keep the UI responsive?
questions.answer:
Short answer: The calculation runs on the main thread, and while it runs the browser cannot handle clicks, typing or painting. Move the work off the main thread with a Web Worker, split it into small chunks, or do it on the server.

How it works:
Web Worker: runs code in a separate thread, talks with postMessage
Chunking: process 1,000 items, then yield with setTimeout or scheduler.yield, repeat
Server: send big jobs to the backend
Faster algorithm: often the real fix (a Map lookup instead of nested loops)
Measure: the Performance tab marks long tasks over 50 ms

Example: Filtering 200,000 rows on every keystroke freezes the search box. Moving the filter into a Web Worker keeps typing smooth, and results appear a moment later.

Common mistake: Wrapping the heavy code in a Promise or async function and expecting it to run in the background. It still runs on the main thread and still freezes the page.

Interview tip: Mention the 50 ms "long task" threshold and the INP Core Web Vital. Using real performance terms makes the answer sound professional.

questions.question: What is requestAnimationFrame, and why is it better than setTimeout for animations?
questions.answer:
Short answer: requestAnimationFrame(callback) runs your callback right before the browser's next repaint, usually 60 times per second (or the screen's refresh rate). It syncs updates with the display, pauses in background tabs and avoids janky, wasted frames.

How it works:
Timing: called once per frame, before style, layout and paint
Timestamp: the callback gets a high-resolution time to calculate progress
Background tabs: paused, saving battery and CPU
setTimeout(16): not synced with the screen, can drift and drop frames
Loop: call requestAnimationFrame again inside the callback for the next frame

Example: A progress bar animated with setTimeout stutters on a busy page. With requestAnimationFrame and time-based progress, it moves smoothly on 60 Hz and 120 Hz screens alike.

Common mistake: Moving an element by a fixed number of pixels per frame. On a 120 Hz screen it moves twice as fast. Base the movement on elapsed time instead.

Interview tip: Mention that CSS transitions and transform animations are often better than any JavaScript loop, because the browser can run them on the compositor thread.

questions.question: What is microtask starvation, and how can a Promise loop freeze a page?
questions.answer:
Short answer: The event loop empties the whole microtask queue before rendering or running the next task. If each microtask schedules another one, the queue never empties, so the page never repaints and timers and clicks never run.

How it works:
Recursive .then or queueMicrotask: keeps adding microtasks forever
No rendering: browsers render only between tasks
No timers or events: macrotasks never get a turn
Different from setTimeout recursion: each setTimeout is a new task, so the browser can render in between

Example: A "polling" function written as function poll() { Promise.resolve().then(poll); } freezes the tab completely. Written with setTimeout(poll, 1000), it runs once per second and the page stays responsive.

Common mistake: Thinking async code can never block the page. Promises run on the same thread, and an endless chain blocks as hard as a while (true) loop.

Interview tip: Compare it with process.nextTick starvation in Node. Showing the same idea on both platforms shows a deep understanding of the event loop.

questions.question: setTimeout(fn1, 0) and Promise.resolve().then(fn2) are scheduled in the same script. Which runs first?
options: fn1, because it was scheduled first
fn2, because Promise callbacks are microtasks
They run at the same time
questions.correctAnswer: fn2, because Promise callbacks are microtasks
questions.answer:
Why B: Microtasks run as soon as the current script finishes, before any macrotask such as a timer.

Why not A: Scheduling order matters only within the same queue.

Why not C: JavaScript runs one callback at a time on the main thread.

Why not D: The order is defined by the event loop rules.

questions.question: What does this print? console.log("A"); setTimeout(() => console.log("B")); Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log("C")); console.log("D");
questions.answer:
Why D: Sync logs first (A, D), then the microtask (C), then the timer (B).

Why not A: Callbacks never run in the middle of synchronous code.

Why not B: C is a callback, so it must wait for D, which is synchronous.

Why not C: The timer (macrotask) waits for all microtasks, so C comes before B.

questions.question: Into which queue does queueMicrotask(fn) put fn?
options: The microtask queue, like Promise callbacks
It runs fn immediately, without a queue
questions.correctAnswer: The microtask queue, like Promise callbacks
questions.answer:
Why C: queueMicrotask adds fn to the same microtask queue that Promise callbacks use.

Why not A: The name says it: it is a microtask, not a macrotask.

Why not B: Rendering is not a queue you add functions to (requestAnimationFrame is the closest).

Why not D: fn runs after the current synchronous code finishes.

questions.question: What does "JavaScript is single-threaded" mean?
options: Your JavaScript code runs on one main thread, one piece at a time
The browser can only make one network request at a time
Only one tab can run JavaScript
questions.correctAnswer: Your JavaScript code runs on one main thread, one piece at a time
questions.answer:
Why A: Your callbacks and functions run one at a time on the main thread, while the environment handles waiting work in the background.

Why not B: The browser makes many network requests in parallel.

Why not C: Each tab has its own JavaScript environment.

Why not D: Async code exists exactly so one thread can handle many waiting tasks.

questions.question: What does this print? async function f() { console.log(1); await null; console.log(2); } f(); console.log(3);
questions.answer:
Why B: The code before await runs immediately (1), the caller continues (3), and the code after await runs as a microtask (2).

Why not A: await pauses the function, even when the awaited value is not a Promise.

Why not C: Calling f() runs its first part right away, before the next line.

Why not D: 2 is logged only after the pause.

questions.question: A setTimeout(fn, 0) is scheduled, then a synchronous loop runs for 2 seconds. When does fn run?
options: After about 0 ms, interrupting the loop
After about 4 ms, the browser minimum
Never, the timer is cancelled by the long loop
After the loop finishes, about 2 seconds later
questions.correctAnswer: After the loop finishes, about 2 seconds later
questions.answer:
Why D: A timer callback can run only when the call stack is empty, so it waits for the loop to end.

Why not A: JavaScript never interrupts running synchronous code.

Why not B: The minimum delay does not matter when the thread is busy for 2 seconds.

Why not C: The timer is not cancelled, it just runs late.

questions.question: What is the DOM, and how does JavaScript use it?
questions.answer:
Short answer: The DOM (Document Object Model) is the browser's tree of objects built from your HTML. Each tag becomes a node that JavaScript can find, read, change, add or remove, and the page updates on screen.

How it works:
Find: document.querySelector('.btn'), getElementById('title')
Read and change: el.textContent, el.classList.add('active'), el.style.color
Create: document.createElement('li'), then parent.append(li)
Remove: el.remove()
Events: el.addEventListener('click', handler)

Example: A "dark mode" button does document.body.classList.toggle('dark'), and CSS for .dark changes the whole page's colours.

Common mistake: Using innerHTML to insert user text. textContent is safe, while innerHTML parses HTML, which can run an attacker's code (XSS).

Interview tip: Mention that React builds a virtual description of the UI and updates the real DOM for you, but understanding the DOM helps you debug React and work with refs.

questions.question: What are event bubbling and capturing, and what does stopPropagation() do?
questions.answer:
Short answer: When you click an element, the event travels down from the window to the target (capturing phase), then back up from the target to the window (bubbling phase). Listeners run in bubbling by default. stopPropagation() stops the event from travelling further.

How it works:
Capturing: window down to the target, listen with { capture: true }
Target: the element that was actually clicked
Bubbling: target up through every parent to the window
stopPropagation(): parents do not receive the event anymore
Not every event bubbles: focus and blur do not (focusin and focusout do)

Example: A card is clickable to open details, and it has a "Delete" button inside. Clicking Delete also bubbles to the card and opens details. Calling e.stopPropagation() in the delete handler fixes it.

Common mistake: Using stopPropagation everywhere. It breaks outside-click detection for dropdowns and analytics that listen on the document.

Interview tip: Mention that bubbling is what makes event delegation possible, which is usually the next question.

questions.question: What is event delegation, and why is it useful?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Instead of adding a listener to every child element, add one listener to a common parent and use event.target to find which child was clicked. It works because events bubble up.

How it works:
One listener: on the parent, like the ul
Find the child: e.target.closest('li') or a data attribute
Dynamic items: works for items added later, no new listeners needed
Memory: one listener instead of hundreds

Example: A todo list with 500 items uses one listener on the list: if (e.target.matches('.delete')) remove(e.target.closest('li').dataset.id). New todos work automatically.

Common mistake: Checking e.target directly when the button has an icon inside. A click on the icon makes e.target the icon, not the button. Use closest('.delete') to find the button.

Interview tip: Mention that React uses a form of delegation internally: it attaches listeners at the root, not on every element.

questions.question: What is the difference between localStorage, sessionStorage and cookies?
questions.answer:
Short answer: localStorage keeps data until it is cleared, sessionStorage keeps it only for one tab session, and cookies are small values that the browser sends to the server with every request. All three store strings only.

How it works:
localStorage: about 5 MB, survives restarts, shared by all tabs of the same origin
sessionStorage: about 5 MB, one tab only, gone when the tab closes
Cookies: about 4 KB each, sent automatically with requests, can be httpOnly
Strings only: use JSON.stringify and JSON.parse for objects
JavaScript access: storage is readable by any script on the page, httpOnly cookies are not

Example: A theme setting goes in localStorage, a multi-step form draft in sessionStorage, and a login session in an httpOnly cookie that JavaScript cannot read.

Common mistake: Storing a JWT in localStorage without thinking about XSS. Any injected script can read it and send it to an attacker.

Interview tip: Mention that storage access can throw in private mode or when it is full, so wrap reads and writes in try/catch.

questions.question: What is the difference between preventDefault() and stopPropagation()?
questions.answer:
Short answer: preventDefault() stops the browser's built-in action for the event, like submitting a form or following a link. stopPropagation() stops the event from reaching parent elements. They solve different problems and can be used together.

How it works:
preventDefault: no page reload on submit, no navigation on link click, no checkbox toggle
stopPropagation: parents' listeners do not run
Both: possible, they do not affect each other
Passive listeners: { passive: true } promises not to call preventDefault, which makes scrolling smoother

Example: A React login form uses onSubmit={(e) => { e.preventDefault(); login(); }} so the page does not reload and lose its state.

Common mistake: Calling stopPropagation in a form submit handler and wondering why the page still reloads. Only preventDefault stops the submit.

Interview tip: Mention e.defaultPrevented, which lets other code check if someone already cancelled the default action.

questions.question: What are reflow and repaint, and how do you update the DOM efficiently?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Reflow (layout) recalculates sizes and positions of elements, repaint redraws pixels. Both cost time. Changing the DOM in a loop, or mixing reads and writes, can force many reflows. Batch your changes and avoid layout thrashing.

How it works:
Triggers reflow: changing size, content or adding elements
Forced reflow: reading offsetHeight or getBoundingClientRect right after a write
Layout thrashing: write, read, write, read in a loop
Batch: build in a DocumentFragment or one string, then insert once
Cheaper changes: transform and opacity skip layout and are good for animation

Example: Adding 1,000 rows one by one with appendChild inside a loop that also reads each row's height takes seconds. Building them in a DocumentFragment and inserting once takes milliseconds.

Common mistake: Animating top and left. They trigger layout on every frame, while transform: translate() does not.

Interview tip: Mention that frameworks like React batch DOM updates for you, which is one reason they feel fast, but you can still cause thrashing in effects and refs.

questions.question: What is the difference between normal script loading, async and defer, and between DOMContentLoaded and load?
questions.answer:
Short answer: A normal script blocks HTML parsing while it downloads and runs. async downloads in parallel and runs as soon as it is ready, in any order. defer downloads in parallel and runs in order after the HTML is parsed. DOMContentLoaded fires when the HTML is parsed, load fires when images and styles are loaded too.

How it works:
Normal: blocks parsing, runs in order
async: does not block, runs when ready, order not guaranteed (good for analytics)
defer: does not block, runs in order before DOMContentLoaded (good for app code)
type="module": deferred by default
