DOMContentLoaded: DOM ready, images may still load
load: everything, including images, has loaded

Example: Moving a big script from a blocking tag in the head to defer cut the time to first content on a landing page by about a second, because the browser could show HTML while the script downloaded.

Common mistake: Putting async on scripts that depend on each other. A plugin can run before the library it needs and throw "jQuery is not defined".

Interview tip: Mention that Vite and modern bundlers use type="module" scripts, which are deferred automatically.
questions.codeSnippet:
<script src="analytics.js" async></script>   <!-- independent -->
<script src="vendor.js" defer></script>      <!-- runs first -->
<script src="app.js" defer></script>         <!-- then this -->

questions.question: How does IntersectionObserver work, and how would you use it for lazy loading or infinite scroll?
questions.answer:
Short answer: IntersectionObserver tells you when an element enters or leaves the viewport (or a container), without listening to scroll events. You use it to load images when they come into view, or to fetch the next page when a "sentinel" element at the bottom becomes visible.

How it works:
Create: new IntersectionObserver(callback, { rootMargin: '200px' })
Observe: observer.observe(element)
Callback: gets entries with isIntersecting
rootMargin: start loading a bit before the element is visible
Cleanup: unobserve or disconnect when done

Example: A question list shows 20 items and an empty div at the bottom. When the div becomes visible, the next 20 load. Scrolling stays smooth because no scroll handler runs on every pixel.

Common mistake: Building infinite scroll with a scroll event listener that calls getBoundingClientRect on every scroll. It runs hundreds of times per second and causes jank.

Interview tip: Mention the native loading="lazy" attribute for images, which covers the simple case without any JavaScript.

questions.question: What is the same-origin policy, and why does a React app on localhost:5173 need CORS to call an API on localhost:5000?
questions.answer:
Short answer: The same-origin policy stops a page from reading responses from a different origin (protocol, host and port). Different ports are different origins, so the browser blocks the response unless the API sends CORS headers that allow the app's origin.

How it works:
Origin: protocol + host + port, like http://localhost:5173
Same origin: all three match
CORS: the server says Access-Control-Allow-Origin: http://localhost:5173
Preflight: for JSON POST or custom headers, the browser sends OPTIONS first
Dev shortcut: Vite's proxy makes requests look same-origin during development

Example: During development, the React app calls http://localhost:5000/api/courses and the console shows "blocked by CORS policy". Adding cors({ origin: 'http://localhost:5173' }) to Express, or a Vite proxy, fixes it.

Common mistake: Trying to fix CORS in the frontend with headers like Access-Control-Allow-Origin on the request. CORS headers must come from the server's response.

Interview tip: Mention that the request often still reaches the server, the browser only hides the response. That is why CORS is not a replacement for authentication.

questions.question: How does a browser turn HTML, CSS and JavaScript into pixels (the critical rendering path)?
questions.answer:
Short answer: The browser parses HTML into the DOM and CSS into the CSSOM, combines them into a render tree, calculates layout (sizes and positions), paints the pixels, and composites the layers on screen. JavaScript can pause this process and trigger it again.

How it works:
DOM: built from HTML as it downloads
CSSOM: built from CSS, which blocks rendering until it loads
Render tree: visible elements with their styles
Layout: exact size and position of every box
Paint: fill in text, colours, borders and images
Composite: combine layers, transforms and opacity here are cheap

Example: A page shows a blank screen for 2 seconds because a large CSS file and a blocking script in the head must load first. Inlining critical CSS and deferring the script makes content appear much sooner.

Common mistake: Thinking JavaScript size is the only performance issue. Render-blocking CSS and fonts can delay the first paint just as much.

Interview tip: Connect it to Core Web Vitals: LCP (largest content paint), CLS (layout shift) and INP (responsiveness). Using these terms shows you know how performance is measured today.

questions.question: Build a star rating widget with plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript (no framework). What do you need to handle?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Render five buttons, keep the selected rating in a variable, highlight stars on hover and click, and use one event listener on the container (event delegation). Make it work with the keyboard and screen readers, and tell the rest of the page when the value changes.

How it works:
State: the saved rating and the hover preview
Event delegation: one listener reads data-value from the clicked star
Hover preview: mouseover shows the preview, mouseleave goes back to the saved value
Accessibility: real <button> elements, aria-label like "3 stars", aria-pressed on the selected one
Output: update a hidden input or dispatch a custom "change" event for the form

Example: A product review form: hovering shows 4 gold stars, clicking saves 4, and leaving the widget keeps 4 highlighted.

Common mistake: Using <div> or <span> stars with only a click handler (no keyboard support), or adding one listener per star.

Interview tip: Talk through state first, then rendering, then events. Interviewers watch whether your render function is driven by state.

questions.question: Build tic-tac-toe in vanilla JavaScript. How do you store the game state and check for a winner?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Keep the game in plain data: an array of 9 cells, the current player and a winner flag. On a click, ignore filled cells, place the mark, check the 8 winning lines, then switch player and re-render from the array.

How it works:
State: board = Array(9).fill(null), player = "X", winner = null
Winning lines: 3 rows, 3 columns and 2 diagonals, stored as index triples
Click: one listener on the board (event delegation) reads data-index
Draw: no winner and no empty cell left
Render: update every cell from the board array, never read the game state from the DOM

Example: X plays 0, 4 and 8. The check finds the line [0, 4, 8] with three X marks and shows "X wins".

Common mistake: Storing the state only in the DOM (reading textContent to find the winner), which makes reset and checks messy.

Interview tip: Mention the next steps you would add: a reset button, highlighting the winning line and keyboard support.

questions.question: Take input from a form, show a message based on the value, and add the data as a new row in a table using plain JavaScript.
questions.answer: Short answer: Listen for the form's submit event, call preventDefault(), read the values with FormData, validate them, show the right message, then build a with textContent (never innerHTML for user input) and reset the form. How it works: submit event: also fires when the user presses Enter preventDefault(): stops the page from reloading FormData(form): reads every named input at once Message: set textContent and a class like "error" or "ok" Table row: insertRow() and insertCell(), with textContent so typed HTML is shown as text Example: A student enters a name and marks. Marks of 50 or more show "Pass" in green, otherwise "Fail" in red, and a new row appears in the results table. Common mistake: Building the row with innerHTML and the user's text. Someone can type and run script (XSS). Interview tip: Mention accessibility: put the message in an element with aria-live="polite" so screen readers announce it.

questions.question: What does document.querySelector(".item") return when several elements have the class "item"?
options: An array of all matching elements
questions.answer:
Why B: querySelector returns only the first element that matches the selector, or null if none match.

Why not A: querySelector never returns an array.

Why not C: It returns the first match in document order, not the last.

Why not D: A NodeList of all matches comes from querySelectorAll.

questions.question: A click listener is on a ul and the user clicks a span inside an li. What are e.target and e.currentTarget?
options: e.target is the span, e.currentTarget is the ul
e.target is the ul, e.currentTarget is the span
questions.correctAnswer: e.target is the span, e.currentTarget is the ul
questions.answer:
Why A: target is the element that was actually clicked, and currentTarget is the element whose listener is running.

Why not B: The two are the other way round.

Why not C: The li is only a parent the event passes through, so it is neither of them here.

Why not D: Only currentTarget is the ul.

questions.question: After localStorage.setItem("count", 5), what does localStorage.getItem("count") return?
questions.answer:
Why C: Web storage stores only strings, so the number is converted to "5".

Why not A: Values come back as strings, so convert with Number() if needed.

Why not B: The key exists, so it is not undefined.

Why not D: null is returned only for keys that do not exist.

questions.question: With default listeners, in what order do click handlers run when a button inside a div is clicked?
options: The div first, then the button
The button first, then the div
questions.correctAnswer: The button first, then the div
questions.answer:
Why D: By default listeners run in the bubbling phase, which goes from the target up to its parents.

Why not A: That happens only for listeners registered with capture: true.

Why not B: The event bubbles to the div too, unless stopPropagation is called.

Why not C: The order is defined by the capture and bubble phases.

questions.question: How do scripts marked with defer run?
options: As soon as each one downloads, in any order
After the HTML is parsed, in the order they appear
Only after all images have loaded
questions.correctAnswer: After the HTML is parsed, in the order they appear
questions.answer:
Why B: defer downloads in parallel without blocking, and runs the scripts in document order once parsing is done, before DOMContentLoaded.

Why not A: That describes async scripts.

Why not C: Deferred scripts wait for parsing to finish.

Why not D: Waiting for images is what the load event is about, not defer.

questions.question: Is data saved in sessionStorage shared between two tabs of the same site?
options: Yes, all tabs of the same origin share it
Yes, but only after a page reload
No, each tab has its own sessionStorage
No, sessionStorage is cleared on every page load
questions.correctAnswer: No, each tab has its own sessionStorage
questions.answer:
Why C: sessionStorage is scoped to a single tab. Opening the site in a new tab starts with an empty sessionStorage.

Why not A: Sharing between tabs is how localStorage behaves.

Why not B: Reloading does not make tabs share data.

Why not D: sessionStorage survives reloads within the same tab.

questions.question: How do try, catch and finally work in JavaScript?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Code in try runs normally. If it throws, the rest of try is skipped and catch runs with the error. finally runs at the end in every case, success or error, and is used for cleanup.

How it works:
try: the code that might fail
catch (err): handles the error, err.message and err.stack are useful
finally: always runs, even after return or a throw in catch
Optional binding: catch { } without a variable is allowed
Rethrow: throw err inside catch if you cannot really handle it

Example: A file upload shows a spinner, tries to upload, shows an error message if it fails, and in finally always hides the spinner, so it never spins forever.

Common mistake: An empty catch block, catch (e) {}. The error disappears silently, and the bug becomes very hard to find later.

Interview tip: Say you catch errors only where you can do something useful (show a message, retry, add context), and let others bubble up to a central handler.

questions.question: What are the main built-in error types, and how do you create a custom error?
questions.answer:
Short answer: The common built-in errors are TypeError, ReferenceError, SyntaxError, RangeError and the general Error. For your own cases, extend Error to add a name and extra fields like a status code.

How it works:
TypeError: using a value the wrong way, like calling undefined or reading a property of null
ReferenceError: using a variable that does not exist (or is in the TDZ)
SyntaxError: invalid code, or JSON.parse on bad text
RangeError: a value out of range, like new Array(-1) or too deep recursion
Custom: class ValidationError extends Error, set this.name

Example: A form validator throws new ValidationError('Email is required', 'email'). The caller checks err instanceof ValidationError and shows the message next to the email field, while unknown errors show a generic message.

Common mistake: Throwing strings, like throw 'Not found'. Strings have no stack trace, so you cannot see where the problem started.

Interview tip: Mention the cause option: new Error('Save failed', { cause: err }) keeps the original error attached, which makes debugging chains of failures much easier.

questions.question: When should a function throw an error, and when should it return a value like null or a result object?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Throw for unexpected problems the caller cannot ignore, like invalid arguments or a failed network call. Return a value (null, false or a result object) for normal, expected outcomes like "user not found" or "form invalid".

How it works:
Throw: bugs, broken input contracts, failures that need handling higher up
Return null: "nothing found" is a normal answer
Result object: { ok: false, errors } when the caller needs details
Consistency: pick one style per layer so callers know what to expect
Never: throw for normal control flow in hot loops (slow and confusing)

Example: findUserByEmail returns null when there is no user, because that is common at login. saveUser throws when the database is down, because the caller cannot continue.

Common mistake: Returning an error message string from a function that normally returns data, like return 'Error: not found'. Callers then treat the error text as real data.

Interview tip: Mention that libraries like zod offer both styles (parse throws, safeParse returns a result), which shows the trade-off is a real design decision.

questions.question: How does garbage collection work in JavaScript?
questions.answer:
Short answer: JavaScript frees memory automatically. The engine regularly finds values that can no longer be reached from the "roots" (global variables, the current call stack, active closures) and frees them. This is called mark-and-sweep.

How it works:
Roots: globals, variables in running functions, things the browser holds (DOM, timers)
Mark: follow every reference from the roots and mark what is reachable
Sweep: free everything that was not marked
Generations: new objects are checked often, long-lived ones less often
Circular references: fine, an unreachable cycle is still freed

Example: After a user closes a modal, its data object is no longer referenced by any variable, listener or component. The next garbage collection frees it.

Common mistake: Thinking setting a variable to null "deletes" the object. It only removes that one reference. If something else still points to the object, it stays in memory.

Interview tip: Say that memory leaks in JavaScript are not "forgetting to free memory", they are "accidentally keeping a reference". That framing leads naturally into how to find leaks.

questions.question: What are the most common causes of memory leaks in front-end JavaScript apps?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Most leaks come from references that live longer than needed: event listeners and timers that are never removed, ever-growing caches or arrays, detached DOM nodes still referenced in variables, and closures held by long-lived objects.

How it works: Usual suspects:
Listeners: window or document listeners added on mount, never removed
Timers: setInterval that keeps running after the component is gone
Global caches: a Map that only grows
Detached DOM: removed elements still stored in a variable or array
Subscriptions: websockets, observers and stores without unsubscribe

Example: A chat component adds a socket.on('message') listener every time it mounts and never removes it. After visiting the page 10 times, each message is handled 10 times and memory keeps growing.

Common mistake: Looking only at big objects. Many small leaks (one listener per visit) add up and slow the app over a long session.

Interview tip: Mention the React pattern: every subscription in useEffect returns a cleanup function. It is the most common real-world fix.

questions.question: How do you find a memory leak with Chrome DevTools?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Reproduce the action that leaks, take heap snapshots before and after repeating it, and compare them. Objects that keep growing (and the reference chains that keep them alive) point to the leak.

How it works: Steps:
Performance monitor: watch JS heap size while repeating an action
Heap snapshot: take one, repeat the action several times, take another
Comparison view: sort by delta to see what keeps growing
Retainers: shows which reference keeps each object alive
Detached elements: search for "Detached" to find removed DOM nodes still in memory
Allocation timeline: shows where new memory is created over time

Example: Opening and closing a modal 10 times adds 10 detached modal elements. The retainers panel shows they are held by a keydown listener on document that was never removed.

Common mistake: Taking one snapshot and guessing. Leaks show up as growth between snapshots, so you always need a comparison.

Interview tip: Mention forcing garbage collection (the trash icon) before each snapshot, so you compare only memory that really cannot be freed.

questions.question: What is the difference between debounce and throttle, and when would you use each?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Debounce waits until events stop for a set time, then runs once. Throttle runs at most once per time window while events keep coming. Debounce is for "when the user is done", throttle is for "regular updates while it happens".

How it works:
Debounce: each new event resets the timer, runs after a quiet period
Throttle: runs, then ignores events until the window passes
Leading or trailing: either can run at the start, the end or both
Typical delays: 300 ms for search, 100 to 200 ms for scroll

Example: A search box uses debounce (300 ms), so it sends one request after typing stops instead of one per letter. A "back to top" button that shows while scrolling uses throttle, checking the scroll position at most every 200 ms.

Common mistake: Creating a new debounced function on every React render. Each render gets a fresh timer, so debouncing never works. Create it once with useMemo or useRef.

Interview tip: Use the elevator analogy for debounce (the door waits until people stop coming) and a machine gun's fire rate for throttle. Then offer to write either one.

questions.question: What is memoization, and what are its trade-offs?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Memoization stores the results of a function call, so the next call with the same input returns the saved result instead of computing again. It trades memory for speed and only makes sense for pure, repeated, expensive calculations.

How it works:
Cache key: built from the arguments, often a string or a Map key
Pure functions only: the same input must always give the same output
Memory: the cache grows, so limit its size (for example LRU)
React: useMemo, useCallback and React.memo are memoization tools
Cheap work: memoizing simple math can be slower than just recalculating

Example: Calculating statistics from 50,000 quiz attempts takes 200 ms. Memoizing by filter settings makes switching between tabs instant, because each result is computed once.

Common mistake: Wrapping every value in useMemo "for performance". Each one costs memory and comparison time, and most render work is already fast.

Interview tip: Say you measure first (React Profiler or console.time), then memoize only what is slow. Measured decisions sound much more senior than "I memoize everything".

questions.question: How do you measure the performance of a web page or a piece of JavaScript code?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Measure small code with performance.now() or console.time, measure the page with the DevTools Performance tab and Lighthouse, and measure real users with Core Web Vitals (LCP, INP, CLS).

How it works:
performance.now(): high-resolution time around a piece of code
console.time / timeEnd: quick timing in development
Performance tab: flame chart of long tasks, layout and paint
Lighthouse: lab scores and specific suggestions
Core Web Vitals: LCP (loading), INP (responsiveness), CLS (visual stability)
Real users: web-vitals library or analytics tools

Example: A product page has a poor LCP. The Performance tab shows a 1.5 MB hero image loading late. Compressing it and adding fetchpriority="high" cuts LCP from 4.2 s to 1.8 s.

Common mistake: Optimizing without measuring, like rewriting loops that take 2 ms while a 3 MB bundle is the real problem.

Interview tip: Always give before and after numbers when you talk about performance work. Concrete numbers make the story believable.

questions.question: Why can try/catch not catch errors from a setTimeout callback or an un-awaited Promise, and how do global error handlers help?
questions.answer:
Short answer: try/catch only catches errors thrown while its block is running. A setTimeout callback runs later, after the try block is finished, and an un-awaited Promise rejects later too. Global handlers (window.onerror, unhandledrejection, or process events in Node) catch what slips through.

How it works:
Timer callbacks: need their own try/catch inside the callback
Promises: await them inside try, or add .catch()
window.addEventListener('error'): uncaught errors in the browser
window.addEventListener('unhandledrejection'): rejected Promises with no handler
Node: process.on('uncaughtException') and 'unhandledRejection'
Use: log and report (for example to Sentry), not to continue as if nothing happened

Example: An analytics call inside setTimeout throws for some users. try/catch around setTimeout catches nothing. A global unhandled error handler reports it, and the team sees the bug the same day.

Common mistake: Using global handlers to hide errors. They are for reporting, while each feature should still handle its own expected errors.

Interview tip: Mention error monitoring tools like Sentry. Saying "I want to know about errors before users report them" is a mindset remote teams value.

questions.question: Where are objects and primitive values stored in memory in JavaScript (stack vs heap)?
questions.answer:
Short answer: A simple model: each function call gets a frame on the call stack that holds its local primitive values and references; objects, arrays and functions live in the heap, and a variable only holds a reference to them. Engines like V8 optimize this in their own ways, but the model explains copy by value vs copy by reference.

How it works:
Stack: one frame per function call, removed when the function returns
Heap: objects; the garbage collector frees them when nothing can reach them any more
let b = a: copies the value for a primitive, but copies only the reference for an object
Closures: variables a closure uses are kept alive (on the heap) after the outer function returns

Example: const user = { name: "Ali" }; const copy = user; copy.name = "Sara"; Now user.name is "Sara" too, because both variables point to the same heap object.

Common mistake: Stating "primitives are always on the stack" as an absolute rule. Long strings and closure variables are heap-allocated in V8. Present it as a mental model.

Interview tip: Connect it to memory leaks: a heap object that is still referenced from a global variable, a cache or an event listener is never freed.

questions.question: When does a finally block run?
options: Only when no error is thrown
Only when an error is caught
Always, whether the try block succeeds or throws
Only if there is no catch block
questions.correctAnswer: Always, whether the try block succeeds or throws
questions.answer:
Why C: finally runs after try (and catch, if any) in every case, which is why it is used for cleanup.

Why not A: It also runs when there is an error.

Why not B: It also runs when everything succeeds.

Why not D: finally works with or without a catch block.

questions.question: const user = null; console.log(user.name); Which error is thrown?
questions.answer:
Why B: Reading a property of null or undefined is using a value the wrong way, which is a TypeError: "Cannot read properties of null".

Why not A: user exists, so it is not a ReferenceError.

Why not C: The code is valid syntax.

Why not D: No number or length is out of range here.

questions.question: console.log(totalPrice); where totalPrice was never declared anywhere. Which error is thrown?
questions.answer:
Why D: Reading a variable that does not exist in any scope throws "totalPrice is not defined", a ReferenceError.

Why not A: TypeError is for using an existing value in the wrong way.

Why not B: The code itself is valid. The problem appears when it runs.

Why not C: Nothing is out of range.

questions.question: Which pattern most likely causes a memory leak in a single-page app?
options: Adding a window resize listener every time a component mounts, and never removing it
Creating many small objects inside a function
questions.correctAnswer: Adding a window resize listener every time a component mounts, and never removing it
questions.answer:
Why A: window lives for the whole session, so each forgotten listener and everything its closure references stays in memory.

Why not B: const and let do not affect memory leaks.

Why not C: Short-lived objects become unreachable and are freed normally.

Why not D: Arrow functions are fine. The problem is keeping references alive too long.

questions.question: What does f() return? function f() { try { return 1; } finally { return 2; } }
questions.answer:
Why B: finally runs after the return in try, and a return inside finally replaces the earlier return value.

Why not A: The return in finally overrides it, which is why returning from finally is discouraged.

Why not C: A value is returned, the one from finally.

Why not D: Returning from finally is allowed, even though it is a bad idea.

questions.question: A try/catch wraps setTimeout(() => { throw new Error("x"); }, 0). What happens when the callback throws?
options: The error is uncaught, because the callback runs after the try block has finished
questions.correctAnswer: The error is uncaught, because the callback runs after the try block has finished
questions.answer:
Why D: The callback runs later as a separate task. The try block has already finished, so its catch cannot see the error.

Why not A: try/catch only covers code that runs while the try block is active.

Why not B: It is reported as an uncaught error in the console (and can crash a Node process).

Why not C: Timers never retry callbacks.

Fix: Put the try/catch inside the callback.

questions.question: Write a function that checks if a string is a palindrome, ignoring case, spaces and punctuation.
questions.answer:
Short answer: Clean the string (lowercase it and keep only letters and digits), then compare it with its reverse, or walk two pointers from both ends toward the middle.

How it works:
Clean: s.toLowerCase().replace(/[^a-z0-9]/g, '')
Simple check: compare with [...clean].reverse().join('')
Two pointers: compare clean[i] and clean[j], move inward, stop at the middle
Complexity: O(n) time, and the two-pointer version avoids building a reversed copy

Example: "A man, a plan, a canal: Panama" becomes "amanaplanacanalpanama", which reads the same both ways, so the function returns true. "Hello" returns false.

Common mistake: Forgetting to clean the input. "Race car" fails because of the space and the capital R, even though it is a palindrome.

Interview tip: Write the simple version first, then offer the two-pointer version and explain why it uses less memory. Showing you can improve your own solution is exactly what interviewers look for.

questions.question: Implement a debounce function.
questions.answer:
Short answer: debounce returns a wrapper that delays calling the original function. Each new call cancels the previous timer and starts a new one, so the function runs only after calls stop for the given delay.

How it works:
Closure: the wrapper remembers the timer id between calls
clearTimeout: cancels the pending call on each new call
setTimeout: schedules the real call after the delay
this and arguments: pass them through with fn.apply(this, args)
Extras: a cancel() method, or a leading option to run on the first call

Example: const search = debounce((q) => fetchResults(q), 300). Typing "react" quickly calls search 5 times, but only one request is sent, 300 ms after the last key.

Common mistake: Losing this or the arguments by calling fn() instead of fn.apply(this, args). Methods that use this then break.

Interview tip: Explain the closure and the timer reset in one sentence, then write the code. Mention that in React you keep the debounced function stable with useMemo or useRef.

questions.question: Implement a throttle function.
questions.answer:
Short answer: throttle returns a wrapper that runs the function at most once per time window. The first call runs right away, and calls during the window are ignored (or the last one is saved and run at the end, in a trailing version).

How it works:
Timestamp version: remember the last run time, run only if enough time has passed
Timer version: block calls while a timer is active
Trailing call: optionally save the latest arguments and run them when the window ends
Use cases: scroll, resize, mousemove, button spam protection

Example: const onScroll = throttle(updateProgressBar, 100). Scrolling fires hundreds of events per second, but the progress bar updates only 10 times per second, which still looks smooth.

Common mistake: Using throttle for a search box. Throttle sends requests while the user is still typing, while debounce waits until they stop, which is what search needs.

Interview tip: Write the timestamp version (it is short), then mention the trailing option. Comparing it with debounce in one line closes the answer well.

questions.question: Write a deepClone function, and explain when you would use structuredClone instead.
questions.answer:
Short answer: A recursive deepClone copies primitives as they are, builds a new array or object, and clones every nested value. In real code, prefer the built-in structuredClone, which also handles Dates, Maps, Sets and circular references.

How it works:
Base case: primitives and null are returned directly
Arrays: map over items and clone each one
Objects: copy each own key with a cloned value
Dates: new Date(value.getTime())
Circular references: track seen objects in a WeakMap
structuredClone: handles most built-in types, but not functions or DOM nodes

Example: Editing a copy of a nested quiz draft (questions with options) in a form. With a deep clone, changes do not touch the saved original until the user clicks Save.

Common mistake: A recursive clone without cycle tracking. An object that references itself makes it recurse forever and crash with "Maximum call stack size exceeded".

Interview tip: Write the basic version, then say "in production I would use structuredClone". Knowing when not to reinvent the wheel is a strong signal.

questions.question: Write a function that flattens a nested array, with an optional depth.
questions.answer:
Short answer: Loop over the items. If an item is an array and depth remains, flatten it recursively one level less and add its items. Otherwise add the item as it is. The built-in arr.flat(depth) does the same.

How it works:
Recursion: flatten(item, depth - 1) for nested arrays
Depth: Infinity flattens everything
reduce or a loop: both work, a loop is easier to read
Built-in: [1, [2, [3]]].flat(Infinity)
Stack version: avoids deep recursion for very deep arrays

Example: Tags from several questions, [['js', 'closures'], ['js', ['async', 'promises']]], flattened and de-duplicated with [...new Set(flatten(tags, Infinity))] give one clean tag list.

Common mistake: Forgetting the depth check and always flattening fully, which fails when the interviewer asks for flat(1) behaviour.

Interview tip: Mention flatMap for the common "map then flatten one level" case, like users.flatMap((u) => u.skills).

questions.question: Write a polyfill for Array.prototype.map.
questions.answer:
Short answer: Create a new array, loop over the original by index, call the callback with (item, index, array) and the optional thisArg, and store each result at the same index. Skip empty slots, like the real map does.

How it works:
this: the array map was called on
Callback check: throw a TypeError if it is not a function
Arguments: (element, index, array)
thisArg: the second argument sets this for the callback
Holes: if (i in arr) skips empty slots in sparse arrays
Result: same length as the original

Example: Old browsers without map got it from polyfills like this one, which is why sites using modern methods could still run on them.

Common mistake: Using push for the results. For sparse arrays the indexes then shift, while the real map keeps the same positions.

Interview tip: Name it myMap on Array.prototype only in the interview, and mention that in real projects you never add methods to built-in prototypes, you use a polyfill library or a bundler instead.

questions.question: Implement your own version of Promise.all.
questions.answer:
Short answer: Return a new Promise. Track how many inputs have resolved, and store each result at its original index. Resolve when all are done, reject on the first rejection, and resolve right away for an empty list.

How it works:
Index order: results[i] keeps the input order, not the finish order
Counter: resolve when completed === items.length
Fail fast: the first rejection rejects the outer Promise
Non-Promise values: Promise.resolve(item) wraps them
Empty input: resolve([]) immediately

Example: myAll([fetchUser(), fetchCourses(), 5]) resolves with [user, courses, 5] even if the courses request finishes first.

Common mistake: Using results.push(value). Fast Promises would then appear before slow ones, and the results would be in the wrong order.

Interview tip: Mention the empty array case and plain values without being asked. Edge cases are exactly what interviewers look for in this question.

questions.question: Write a polyfill for Function.prototype.bind.
questions.answer:
Short answer: bind returns a new function that calls the original with a fixed this and any preset arguments, followed by the arguments given later. A complete polyfill also handles being called with new.

How it works:
Save: the original function (this inside myBind) and the preset arguments
Return: a function that calls original.apply(context, [...preset, ...later])
Partial application: preset arguments come first
new: if called with new, ignore the bound this and use the new object
Prototype: keep the original's prototype for new to work

Example: const greetAli = greet.myBind({ name: 'Ali' }, 'Hello'); greetAli('!') returns "Hello Ali!", the same as the built-in bind.

Common mistake: Forgetting the later arguments, so partially applied functions lose the values passed at call time.

Interview tip: Write the basic version first, then mention the new case as an extra. Interviewers usually care most about this, apply and argument merging.

questions.question: Implement a memoize function that works with several arguments and limits the cache size.
questions.answer:
Short answer: Build a cache key from all the arguments, keep results in a Map, and when the Map gets too big, delete the oldest entry. Map keeps insertion order, so the first key is the oldest, and re-inserting on a hit keeps recently used items fresh (a simple LRU).

How it works:
Key: JSON.stringify(args) works for simple values (numbers, strings, plain objects)
Map: get, set and has are fast
LRU: on a hit, delete and set again to move the key to the end
Limit: if size > max, delete map.keys().next().value
Pure functions only: memoizing functions with side effects gives wrong results

Example: A price calculator memoize(calcShipping, 100) remembers the last 100 (weight, city) combinations, so repeated cart updates do not recalculate, and memory stays bounded.

Common mistake: An unbounded cache in a long-running Node server. It grows with every unique input until the process runs out of memory.

Interview tip: Mention that JSON keys treat {a:1,b:2} and {b:2,a:1} as different, and that object arguments may need a custom key function. Pointing out limitations shows maturity.

questions.question: Implement a simple EventEmitter with on, off, once and emit.
questions.answer:
Short answer: Keep a Map from event names to arrays (or Sets) of listeners. on adds a listener, off removes it, emit calls every listener with the arguments, and once wraps a listener so it removes itself after the first call.

How it works:
Storage: Map of event name to a list of functions
on: add the function, return this for chaining (or an unsubscribe function)
off: filter the function out
emit: copy the list first, then call each listener (so off during emit is safe)
once: a wrapper that calls off before running the real listener

Example: A chat client emits "message" when a socket message arrives. The chat window, the unread badge and the sound player each subscribe with on, without knowing about each other.

Common mistake: Looping over the live listener array in emit while a once listener removes itself. The array changes during the loop and the next listener is skipped.

Interview tip: Mention that Node's EventEmitter and the browser's EventTarget work this way. Linking your code to real APIs shows you understand where the pattern is used.

questions.question: Delete a node from a singly linked list when you only have a reference to that node (not the head).
questions.answer:
Short answer: You cannot reach the previous node, so copy the next node's value into the given node and then skip the next node. It runs in O(1).

How it works:
node.value = node.next.value: the given node takes the next value
node.next = node.next.next: the next node drops out of the list
This does not work for the last node, because there is no next value to copy

Example: List 4 -> 5 -> 1 -> 9 and you get the node 5. Copy 1 into it (4 -> 1 -> 1 -> 9), then skip the old 1, giving 4 -> 1 -> 9.

Common mistake: Forgetting the last-node case, or trying to walk from a head you do not have.

Interview tip: Say the limitation out loud: the node object stays but its value changes, so any other code holding a reference to the removed node now points outside the list.

questions.question: Implement merge sort in JavaScript. What are the time complexities of common sorting algorithms, and what does Array.prototype.sort use?
questions.answer:
Short answer: Merge sort splits the array into halves, sorts each half recursively and merges the two sorted halves. It is O(n log n) in every case, needs O(n) extra memory and is stable.

How it works:
Bubble, selection, insertion sort: O(n^2); insertion sort is O(n) on an almost sorted array
Merge sort: O(n log n) always, stable, extra memory
Quick sort: O(n log n) on average, O(n^2) in the worst case, sorts in place
Array.prototype.sort: V8 uses TimSort (merge + insertion sort), stable since ES2019; without a compare function it compares values as strings

Example: [10, 9, 1].sort() returns [1, 10, 9] because "10" comes before "9" as text. Use .sort((a, b) => a - b) for numbers.

Common mistake: Calling sort() on numbers without a compare function, or saying quick sort is always O(n log n).

Interview tip: When asked to "just explain the concept", state the idea, the complexity and the stability in one breath, then offer to code it.

questions.question: Insert a value into a sorted circular linked list.
questions.answer:
Short answer: Walk around the circle looking for a gap where prev.value <= x <= next.value. If you reach the "turning point" (where prev.value > next.value, the largest value wraps to the smallest), insert there when x is a new maximum or minimum. If you come back to the start without finding a place (all values equal), insert anywhere.

How it works:
Empty list: the new node points to itself and becomes the head
Normal gap: prev.value <= x && x <= next.value
Turning point: prev.value > next.value and (x >= prev.value || x <= next.value)
Full loop: stop when you return to the head, then insert after prev
Time O(n), extra space O(1)

Example: List 3 -> 4 -> 1 (circular), insert 2: the gap 1 -> 3 is found because 1 <= 2 <= 3, giving 3 -> 4 -> 1 -> 2.

Common mistake: Looping forever because there is no stop condition when all values are equal, or forgetting the empty-list case.

Interview tip: List the edge cases before coding: empty list, one node, new max or min, all values equal.

questions.question: Which built-in function makes a deep copy of an object, including nested objects, Dates and Maps?
questions.answer:
Why C: structuredClone copies nested values deeply and supports Dates, Maps, Sets and circular references.

Why not A: Object.assign makes only a shallow copy.

Why not B: Spread also makes only a shallow copy.

Why not D: freeze makes an object read-only, it does not copy anything.

questions.question: A search box uses a debounced function with a 300 ms delay. The user types 5 letters quickly. How many times does the function run?
options: Once, about 300 ms after the last letter
Once, right after the first letter
It never runs while the page is open
questions.correctAnswer: Once, about 300 ms after the last letter
questions.answer:
Why B: Each keystroke resets the timer, so the function runs only after typing stops for 300 ms.

Why not A: That is what happens without debounce.

Why not C: Running on the first call is the leading option, not the default debounce behaviour.

Why not D: It runs once the user pauses.

questions.question: What does [1, [2, [3, [4]]]].flat() return?
questions.answer:
Why A: flat() without an argument flattens only one level.

Why not B: Full flattening needs flat(Infinity).

Why not C: One level is always flattened, so the array changes.

Why not D: That would need flat(2).

questions.question: Which statement best describes throttle?
options: It waits until events stop, then runs once
It cancels every call after the first one forever
It queues all calls and runs them one by one later
It runs the function at most once per time window while events keep coming
questions.correctAnswer: It runs the function at most once per time window while events keep coming
questions.answer:
Why D: Throttle limits the rate: one run per window, no matter how many events happen.

Why not A: That describes debounce.

Why not B: Throttle allows a new run after each window, not just once.

Why not C: Ignored calls are dropped, not queued.

questions.question: function f() { return this.x; } const b = f.bind({ x: 1 }); What does b.bind({ x: 2 })() return?
questions.answer:
Why C: A bound function's this is fixed forever. Binding it again creates another wrapper, but the inner call still uses { x: 1 }.

Why not A: The second bind cannot change the this set by the first.

Why not B: this is { x: 1 }, so this.x has a value.

Why not D: Binding a bound function is allowed, it just has no effect on this.

questions.question: What does Promise.all([]) do?
options: Resolves immediately with an empty array
Never settles, because there is nothing to wait for
questions.correctAnswer: Resolves immediately with an empty array
questions.answer:
Why A: With nothing to wait for, Promise.all is already complete and resolves with [].

Why not B: The spec handles the empty case by resolving at once.

Why not C: An empty array is valid input.

Why not D: The result is always an array, empty here.
